description:
Header files provide declarations for functions, classes, objects, and other features that can be used in a C++ program.

The #include directive tells the preprocessor to include the contents of a header file before the program is compiled.

Standard C++ header files are included using angle brackets, such as #include <iostream>.

Different header files provide different features. For example, <iostream> provides input and output features such as cin and cout, while <iomanip> provides formatting features such as setw() and setprecision().

A program should include the header files needed for the features it uses. Only include header files that are needed by the program. Including unnecessary header files adds additional code for the preprocessor and compiler to process, which can increase compile time and make program dependencies less clear.
syntax: #include <headerFile>
examples:
Include the iostream header for standard input and output.
#include <iostream>

description:
The <iostream> header file provides features for standard input and output.

It provides objects such as cin for input and cout for output, along with other stream features used to communicate with the user.
syntax: #include <iostream>

description:
The <iomanip> header file provides I/O manipulator functions used to control the formatting of input and output.

Common features provided by <iomanip> include setw(), setprecision(), and setfill(). These can be used to control field width, floating-point precision, and fill characters.
syntax: #include <iomanip>

description:
The <string> header file provides the string class and related features used to store and manipulate text.

A string can contain a sequence of characters and provides functions for examining and modifying the stored text.

Features provided by <string> include the string class, string functions, and to_string().
syntax: #include <string>

description:
The <fstream> header file provides classes used to read data from files and write data to files.

The ifstream class is used for file input, the ofstream class is used for file output, and the fstream class can be used for both input and output.

File streams allow many of the same input and output operations used with cin and cout to be performed with files.
syntax: #include <fstream>

description:
The <cmath> header file provides mathematical functions used to perform common mathematical calculations.

These functions can be used for operations such as calculating powers, square roots, absolute values, and rounding values.

Common functions provided by <cmath> include:
- sqrt(x) - Returns the square root of x.
- pow(base, exponent) - Raises a value to a specified power.
- fabs(x) - Returns the absolute value of a floating-point number.
- abs(x) - Returns the absolute value of an integer.
- ceil(x) - Rounds a value up to the next whole number.
- floor(x) - Rounds a value down to the previous whole number.
- round(x) - Rounds a value to the nearest whole number.

The <cmath> library contains many additional mathematical functions beyond those listed above. These are the functions most commonly used in this course.
syntax: #include <cmath>

description:
The <cstdlib> header file provides several general-purpose functions.

For this class, <cstdlib> is primarily used for generating pseudorandom numbers using rand() and setting the starting seed using srand().

The rand() function generates a pseudorandom integer, while srand() sets the seed used by rand().
syntax: #include <cstdlib>

description:
The <ctime> header file provides functions and types used to work with date and time information.

For this class, <ctime> is primarily used for the time() function. The current time can be used with srand() to provide a changing seed for pseudorandom number generation.

Using a changing seed allows rand() to generate a different pseudorandom sequence each time the program runs.
syntax: #include <ctime>

description:
The <cctype> header file provides functions used to examine and convert individual characters.

Character functions can determine whether a character has a particular property, such as being a digit or whitespace character. Other functions can convert letters between uppercase and lowercase.

Functions used in this class include isdigit(), isspace(), toupper(), and tolower().
syntax: #include <cctype>

description:
The <vector> header file provides the vector class, which is used to store a collection of values of the same data type.

Unlike a traditional array, a vector can change its size while the program is running. Vectors also provide functions that can be used to add, remove, access, and examine elements.
syntax: #include <vector>

description:
The <algorithm> header file provides functions for performing common operations on collections of data.

These algorithms can perform operations such as sorting, searching, counting, and rearranging values.

Many algorithms operate on a range of elements specified by iterators. For containers such as vectors, the begin() and end() functions can be used to provide the beginning and end of the range.

Functions used in this class include sort(), find(), copy(), and copy_n().
syntax: #include <algorithm>

Comments are notes written in the source code to provide information about the program.

Comments are ignored by the compiler and do not affect how the program runs. They are used to document code, explain its purpose, and make the program easier to read and understand.

A single-line comment begins with //. Everything after // on that line is treated as a comment.

A multi-line comment begins with /* and ends with */. Everything between these symbols is treated as a comment and can span multiple lines.

Comments should explain the purpose or reasoning behind code when it is not obvious. Avoid unnecessary comments that simply repeat what the code already clearly shows.

For Professor Raymond's class some of the code you will need to comment are the following: conditions/expressions (in ifs and loops), formulas, case statements, and the description or purpose of a function.
examples:
Place a comment after a statement.
const double TAX_RATE = 0.0825;   // Current tax rate

description:
A header comment is a comment placed at the beginning of a source code file that provides general information about the program.

A header comment commonly includes information such as the programmer's name, the programming language the program is written in, the date, and a brief description of the program's purpose.

Header comments provide documentation about the program as a whole rather than explaining a specific statement or section of code.

The exact information included in a header comment may depend on the documentation standards or requirements for the course or organization.For Professor Raymond's class the assignment should also be in the header comment.
syntax:
/*
    Programmer: programmerName
    Date: date
    Language: language
    Assignment: module, lab, lab title
    Description: briefDescription
*/
examples:
A header comment describing a program, using a block comment.
/*
    Programmer: Alex Smith
    Date: July 31, 2026
    Language: C++
    Assignment: Module 2, Lab 1, Grade Calculator
    Description: Calculates and displays a student's average grade.
*/

description:
Word wrap is a feature of a code editor that automatically displays a long line of code on multiple lines when it is too wide to fit within the editor window.

Word wrap changes only how the code is displayed in the editor. It does not add newline characters to the source code and does not affect how the program is compiled or executed.

Although word wrap can make long lines easier to view, programmers should avoid unnecessarily long lines of code. Statements can often be formatted across multiple lines to improve readability.

Word wrap should not be confused with output wrapping. Word wrap affects how source code is displayed in the editor, not how text is displayed by the running program.

Word wrap can also affect how code looks when copied into a MS Word, PDF, or text document; something that might be done for documentation purposes. When program files are submitted to Canvas word wrap is possible.

Coding standards are a set of guidelines used to keep source code consistent, readable, and easy to maintain.

Coding standards may specify how code should be formatted and documented, including naming conventions, indentation, whitespace, comments, line length, and the organization of program statements.

Following consistent coding standards makes programs easier to read and understand, especially when multiple programmers are working with the same code.

Coding standards can vary between courses, organizations, and development teams. When a specific set of coding standards is provided, those standards should be followed consistently throughout the program.
syntax: There is no associated syntax for coding standards.

description:
The std namespace contains names from the C++ Standard Library, including commonly used features such as cout, cin, string, vector, and many standard functions.

By default, names in the std namespace can be accessed by placing std:: before the name, such as std::cout or std::string. The :: symbol is the scope resolution operator.

The statement using namespace std; is called a using directive. A using directive makes names from the std namespace available without requiring std:: before each name.

C++ also provides a using declaration. A using declaration makes a specific name from a namespace available without requiring the namespace name and scope resolution operator. For example, using std::cout; allows cout to be used without writing std::cout, while other members of the std namespace still require std:: unless they are also included in a using declaration.

The difference can be summarized as:

Using Directive
    using namespace std;
    → Makes names from the std namespace available

Using Declaration
    using std::cout;
    → Makes the selected name cout available

Using namespace std can make introductory programs easier to read and write. However, in larger programs it can create naming conflicts when the same name exists in multiple namespaces. Because of this, many coding standards prefer explicitly using std:: or using declarations for specific names.

For Professor Raymond's class, the use of using namespace std; is explicitly required.

Indentation is the use of spaces or tabs at the beginning of a line of code to visually show the structure and nesting of a program.

Statements inside a block of code should be indented one level from the statements surrounding the block. Additional nested blocks should be indented an additional level.

Indentation does not normally affect how a C++ program executes, but consistent indentation makes the structure of the program easier to see and the code easier to read and maintain.

Unlike C++, some programming languages use indentation as part of their syntax. For example, Python uses indentation to define blocks of code instead of curly braces. Incorrect indentation in Python can change the meaning of the code or cause an error.

A code block is a group of statements that are treated as a single unit.

In C++, a code block begins with an opening curly brace { and ends with a closing curly brace }. Code blocks are commonly used with functions, selection statements, and loops.

Variables declared inside a code block have block scope and normally exist only within that block. Nested code blocks can also be created inside other code blocks.

Statements within a code block should be indented to make the structure of the program easier to read.

Curly braces { } are symbols used in C++ to mark the beginning and end of a code block.

The opening curly brace { begins the block, and the closing curly brace } ends the block. All statements between the braces belong to that block.

Curly braces are commonly used to define the bodies of functions, selection statements, loops, classes, structures, and other code blocks.

Opening and closing curly braces must be properly matched. Missing or misplaced braces can change the structure of the program or cause compiler errors.

Indentation should be used with curly braces to make the beginning, end, and nesting of code blocks easy to identify.

For Professor Raymond's class the curly braces must be lined up as part of the coding standards.

The main() function is the starting point of a C++ program. When the program is run, execution begins with the statements inside main().

A C++ program normally contains one main() function. Other functions may be called from main() or from other functions as the program executes.

The main() function has a return type of int, meaning it returns an integer value to the operating system when the program finishes.

Returning 0 indicates that the program completed successfully. In C++, reaching the closing curly brace of main() without a return statement automatically returns 0.

Program structure refers to the overall organization of a C++ program and how its components are arranged.

Although programs vary in size and complexity, the programs written in this course generally follow a consistent structure.

A typical program for this course is organized in the following order:
- Header comment
- #include directives
- User-defined namespace definitions (when used)
- Structure definitions (when used)
- Enumerations (when used)
- Global variables/constants (when used)
- Function prototypes
- The main() function
- Function definitions

Each section is placed before it is needed by the compiler. For example, structures are defined before they are used as global variables or function parameters, and function prototypes are declared before they are called from main().

Following a consistent program structure makes source code easier to read, understand, test, debug, and maintain. As programs become larger, good program organization becomes increasingly important.

As programs become larger, good program structure becomes increasingly important for organizing code and separating related tasks.

Whitespace refers to characters that create space in source code, including spaces, tabs, and newlines.

In C++, whitespace is generally used to separate parts of a statement and to make source code easier to read. In most situations, multiple whitespace characters are treated the same as a single whitespace character.

Whitespace can be used to indent code, separate operators and values, and add blank lines between sections of a program. Consistent use of whitespace improves the readability and organization of code.

Whitespace is required in some situations to separate tokens that would otherwise be interpreted as a single token. For example, a data type and variable name must be separated.

Whitespace inside string and character literals is part of the data and can affect program output.
syntax: int number = 10;
examples:
Whitespace separates parts of a statement.
int number = 10;

Whitespace is required when two tokens must be separated.
int number;      // Valid
intnumber;       // A different identifier, not an int named number

description:
A statement is a complete instruction that tells the computer to perform an action.

A program consists of one or more statements that are executed in sequence unless the program's logic changes the order of execution.

Most C++ statements end with a semicolon (;). However, some language constructs, such as if statements, loops, function definitions, and class definitions, use code blocks enclosed in curly braces instead of ending with a semicolon.

Different types of statements perform different tasks, such as declaring variables, assigning values, performing calculations, calling functions, displaying output, receiving input, making decisions, and repeating actions.

Statements can be grouped into code blocks using curly braces to indicate that they belong together.

A semicolon (;) is used to mark the end of most C++ statements.

When the compiler encounters a semicolon, it knows that the current statement has ended and the next statement begins.

Many statements require a semicolon, including variable declarations, assignment statements, function calls, input statements, output statements, and return statements.

Not every line of C++ code ends with a semicolon. Language constructs such as if statements, loops, function definitions, and namespaces use code blocks enclosed in curly braces rather than ending with a semicolon.

Placing a semicolon where one does not belong can change the behavior of a program or cause logic errors. Forgetting a required semicolon usually results in a compiler error.

An error is a mistake in a program that prevents it from working correctly or producing the expected result.

Programming errors are commonly divided into three categories:

Syntax errors - Errors that violate the rules (syntax) of the C++ language. These errors are detected by the compiler and must be corrected before the program can be compiled. Examples include missing semicolons, unmatched curly braces, misspelled keywords, invalid identifiers, and assigning a value of an incompatible data type.

Runtime errors - Errors that occur while a program is executing. The program compiles successfully, but an error occurs during execution. Examples include dividing by zero, opening a file that does not exist, or accessing memory that is not valid.

Logic errors (also called semantic errors) - Errors in the program's logic or algorithm. The program compiles and executes successfully, but produces incorrect results because the program does not perform the intended calculations or operations. Examples include using an incorrect formula, forgetting parentheses in an expression, or using the wrong comparison operator in an if statement.

One of the most important debugging skills is determining which type of error has occurred before attempting to fix it.

Syntax is the set of rules that defines how statements and other elements of a programming language must be written.

Just as spoken languages have rules for arranging words and punctuation, programming languages have rules for arranging keywords, identifiers, operators, symbols, and other elements of code.

Code that does not follow the syntax rules of C++ can cause a syntax error and prevent the program from compiling.

Examples of syntax rules include using semicolons to end many statements, matching curly braces around code blocks, using parentheses where required, and following the rules for valid identifiers.

Readability refers to how easy source code is for a programmer to read, understand, and follow.

Readable code makes the purpose and structure of a program clear without requiring the reader to spend unnecessary time determining what the code is doing.

Readability can be improved by using meaningful names, consistent indentation, appropriate whitespace, clear comments, logical organization, and consistent coding standards.

Statements should be formatted so they are easy to follow, and unnecessarily complicated expressions or overly long lines should be avoided when a clearer solution is available.

Readable code is especially important when programs are maintained, debugged, modified, or shared with other programmers. Code is often read many more times than it is originally written.

Readability generally does not change how a C++ program executes, but it can greatly affect how easy the program is to understand and maintain.

Code formatting refers to how source code is visually arranged and organized to make it easier to read and understand.

Formatting includes the use of indentation, whitespace, blank lines, line breaks, and the placement of curly braces. Consistent formatting helps make the structure of a program easy to identify.

Code formatting generally does not change how a C++ program executes, but poorly formatted code can make the program difficult to read, understand, debug, and maintain.

Formatting conventions may vary between courses, organizations, and development teams. A chosen formatting style should be applied consistently throughout a program.

Code formatting is one part of coding standards and contributes to overall code readability.

Program documentation is information created to describe the purpose, design, operation, use, and maintenance of a program or software system.

In this course, program documentation primarily refers to documentation within the source code that helps programmers understand the purpose, structure, and operation of a program.

Documentation can include header comments, comments that explain important sections of code, and documentation describing the purpose and use of functions.

Meaningful names for variables, functions, classes, and other identifiers also help make code self-documenting and easier to understand.

Good documentation should provide useful information that is not already obvious from the code. Comments that simply repeat what a clear statement already shows are usually unnecessary.

Consistent formatting, indentation, and organization also contribute to making a program easier to read and maintain.

Program documentation can also include documents created during the design, development, and use of a software system, such as requirements and design documentation, UML diagrams, pseudocode, system manuals, and user manuals. These forms of documentation are beyond the scope of this course and are covered in more detail in courses such as Systems Analysis and Design.

Pseudocode is an informal way of describing the steps and logic of a program before writing the actual code.

Pseudocode uses plain language to describe what a program should do. It allows a programmer to focus on the logic of a solution without being concerned with the exact syntax of a programming language.

There is no single required syntax for pseudocode, but statements typically begin with an action verb, such as INPUT, DISPLAY, CALCULATE, SET, or REPEAT. Beginning statements with a verb makes each step clearly describe the action that should be performed.

Pseudocode should describe the program logic without using programming-language-specific syntax. Symbols and syntax such as semicolons, curly braces, cout, cin, and data type declarations are generally avoided. Indentation can be used to show the structure of selections and loops.

Pseudocode is often created during program design and can be translated into a programming language, such as C++, Java, or Python, after the logic has been developed.

Pseudocode can also be converted into a flowchart because both are used to represent the steps and logic of an algorithm. Pseudocode describes the logic using written statements, while a flowchart represents the same logic visually using symbols and connecting arrows.

Pseudocode is not compiled or executed by the computer and is intended to be read and understood by people.
syntax: ACTION description of the step
examples:
Pseudocode for calculating the average of two grades.
INPUT first grade
INPUT second grade
CALCULATE average of the two grades
DISPLAY average

Pseudocode containing a selection.
INPUT grade
IF grade is greater than or equal to 70
    DISPLAY "Passing"
ELSE
    DISPLAY "Not Passing"
END IF

Pseudocode containing a loop.
SET number to 1
WHILE number is less than or equal to 5
    DISPLAY number
    INCREASE number by 1
END WHILE

description:
A flowchart is a visual diagram used to represent the steps and logic of an algorithm or process.

Flowcharts use standardized shapes connected by arrows to show the order in which actions are performed, where decisions are made, and how the program moves from one step to another.

Common flowchart symbols include:
- Oval or terminator - represents the start or end of the flowchart.
- Rectangle - represents a process, calculation, assignment, or other action.
- Parallelogram - represents input or output, such as receiving user input or displaying information.
- Diamond - represents a decision or condition where the flow can follow different paths.
- Arrow - shows the direction of program flow from one step to another.
- Circle - can be used as a connector between different parts of a flowchart.

Flowcharts and pseudocode can represent the same program logic in different ways. Pseudocode describes the logic using written steps, while a flowchart represents those steps visually using symbols and connecting arrows. Because of this, pseudocode can often be converted directly into a flowchart.

For additional information and examples of flowchart symbols, visit: https://www.lucidchart.com/pages/examples/flowchart_software/

A program algorithm is a finite, ordered set of steps used to solve a problem or accomplish a task.

An algorithm describes what must be done and the order in which the steps should be performed. The algorithm is developed before or independently of the specific programming language used to implement it.

A good algorithm should have clearly defined steps, produce the expected result, and eventually end.

Algorithms can include sequence, selection, and repetition. Sequence performs steps in order, selection chooses between different actions based on a condition, and repetition performs steps multiple times.

An algorithm can be represented using tools such as pseudocode or a flowchart and can then be translated into program code.

The term algorithm should not be confused with the C++ <algorithm> header file, which provides functions for performing operations such as sorting, searching, and copying data.

Program logic is the reasoning that determines how a program processes information and decides what actions to perform.

Program logic determines the order in which statements execute, the conditions used to make decisions, and when actions should be repeated.

The three basic control structures used to organize program logic are sequence, selection, and repetition. Sequence executes statements in order, selection chooses between different paths based on a condition, and repetition executes statements multiple times.

Program logic is part of an algorithm. An algorithm describes the overall steps used to solve a problem, while program logic determines how those steps are organized and how decisions and repetition are handled.

Program logic can be planned using pseudocode or flowcharts before the solution is translated into program code.

Program design is the process of planning how a program will solve a problem before writing the program code.

Program design begins with understanding the problem and identifying what the program must accomplish. The programmer can then identify the required input, processing, and output and develop an algorithm that describes the steps needed to solve the problem.

Tools such as pseudocode and flowcharts can be used to plan and organize the program logic before the algorithm is translated into a programming language.

For larger programs, design may also include dividing the program into smaller components, determining how those components interact, and identifying the data that must be stored and processed.

Careful program design can make a program easier to write, test, debug, understand, and maintain.

Compile time and run time describe two different stages involved in creating and executing a program.

Compile time occurs when the compiler translates the source code into executable code. During this stage, the compiler checks the program for problems such as syntax errors and certain type-related errors. If a compile-time error occurs, the program must be corrected before it can be successfully compiled.

Run time occurs when the compiled program is actually executing. During this stage, statements are executed, variables receive values, user input is processed, calculations are performed, and decisions are made based on the data available while the program is running.

Some problems cannot be detected until run time because they depend on conditions that exist only while the program is executing. These are commonly called run-time errors.

A simple way to distinguish the two is: compile time is when the program is being translated and checked by the compiler; run time is when the compiled program is actually executing.

An identifier is a programmer-defined name used to identify an element in a program.

Identifiers can be used to name variables, constants, functions, structures, classes, objects, namespaces, enumerations, and other program elements.

A valid identifier can contain letters, digits, and underscores (_), but it cannot begin with a digit.

Identifiers cannot contain spaces or special characters, such as -, @, #, or %. They also cannot be C++ keywords, such as int, double, if, while, or return.

Identifiers are case-sensitive. For example, grade, Grade, and GRADE are three different identifiers.

Although an underscore can be used in an identifier, avoid beginning an identifier with an underscore because some underscore-prefixed names are reserved by C++.

These rules determine whether an identifier is valid. Naming conventions, such as using camelCase or PascalCase, are coding standards rather than requirements of the C++ language.

Keywords are words that have a predefined meaning in the C++ language. The compiler recognizes these words as part of the language and uses them to define the structure and behavior of a program.

Keywords are reserved by the C++ language and cannot be used as identifiers. For example, a variable, function, class, or other identifier cannot be named int, while, return, or class.

Examples of C++ keywords include data types (such as int, double, and bool), control statements (such as if, else, switch, while, and for), and other language features (such as return, const, namespace, and class).

As you learn C++, you will encounter additional keywords. Each keyword has a specific purpose and must be used according to the rules of the language.

A variable is a named location in memory used to store data. Every variable has a data type, a name, and a value.

A variable's data type determines the kind of data it can store, such as integers, floating-point numbers, characters, or strings.

A variable name should be descriptive and indicate the purpose of the data it stores. For example, studentName and totalScore are more meaningful than x or a.

Variables are used to store information that may change while a program is running. New values can be assigned to a variable as the program executes.

Variable names are identifiers and must follow the rules for valid C++ identifiers. See the Identifiers topic for the rules governing valid names and the Naming Conventions topic for recommended naming styles.
syntax:
dataType variableName;

dataType variableName = initialValue;
examples: int age = 25;
double price = 19.95;
string name = "Alice";
bool passed = true;

description:
Naming conventions are guidelines for consistently naming variables, constants, functions, classes, and other identifiers in a program.

Naming conventions make code easier to read and help programmers identify the purpose or type of an identifier. Different courses, organizations, and development teams may use different naming conventions.

Common naming conventions include:

camelCase - The first word begins with a lowercase letter and each additional word begins with an uppercase letter. Example: totalPrice

PascalCase - Each word begins with an uppercase letter. Example: StudentRecord

snake_case - Words are lowercase and separated with underscores. Example: total_price

SCREAMING_SNAKE_CASE - Words are uppercase and separated with underscores. Example: MAX_STUDENTS

Hungarian notation - A prefix is added to a name to indicate its data type, object type, or purpose. Examples include intNum for an integer, txtName for a text box, and btnSubmit for a button. Hungarian notation is less commonly used to identify basic data types in modern programming, but prefixes are still used in some coding standards, particularly for identifying GUI controls.

The naming convention used does not change how the program works, but a consistent naming style improves readability and maintainability.

Operators are symbols or keywords that perform operations on one or more operands to produce a result.

An operand is a value, variable, constant, or expression on which an operator acts. For example, in the expression total + tax, the + symbol is the operator, while total and tax are the operands.

C++ provides many categories of operators, including arithmetic operators, assignment operators, comparison operators, logical operators, increment and decrement operators, bitwise operators, and the conditional (ternary) operator.

Operators have different levels of precedence that determine the order in which expressions are evaluated. Parentheses can be used to override the default order of evaluation.

Each operator has a specific purpose and must be used with operands that are appropriate for that operator.

The scope resolution operator :: is used to identify the scope where a name is defined.

It can be used to access a name contained within a namespace. For example, std::cout identifies cout as belonging to the std namespace.

The scope resolution operator can also be used with programmer-defined namespaces and to define class member functions outside of the class definition.

The name before :: identifies the scope, and the name after :: identifies a member of that scope.
syntax: scopeName::memberName
examples:
Access cout from the std namespace.
std::cout << "Hello";

Access a function from a programmer-defined namespace.
Geometry::area();

description: A data type tells C++ what kind of value a variable stores, how much memory may be needed, and what operations can be performed.
syntax: Data types do not have a syntax by themselves. See the related topics for situations where data types would be found.
examples:
short - holds whole numbers, 2-bytes in size
int - holds whole numbers, 4-bytes in size
long - holds whole numbers, 8-bytes in size
float - holds floating point numbers (has decimal places), 4-bytes in size
double - holds floating point numbers (has decimal places), 8-bytes in size
char - holds a single character, 1-bytes in size
bool - holds a true/false - on/off - 1/0 value, 1-bytes in size
string - holds a series of characters, varies in size

NOTE: Most of these data types have an unsigned version as well. This may have been discussed in class, but you likely won't need it for the course.

description:
A user-defined data type is a data type created by the programmer rather than one of the fundamental data types provided by C++.

User-defined data types allow programmers to create types that represent the data needed by a program. They can make programs easier to organize, understand, and maintain by grouping related information or giving meaningful names to sets of values.

The user-defined data types covered in this course include:
- Structures - group related data into a single type.
- Classes - group related data and functions into a single type and provide features for controlling access to the data.
- Enumerations - define a type consisting of a set of named constant values.

Once a user-defined data type has been defined, variables of that type can be declared and used in much the same way as variables of built-in data types.
A constant is a named value that cannot be changed after it is initialized. C++ uses const to define constants. Constants, as a defacto standard, or declared in SCREAMING_SNAKE_CASE
syntax: const dataType CONSTANT_NAME = value;
examples: const double TAX_RATE = 0.0825;
const int MAX_STUDENTS = 30;
const double PI = 3.141592653589793;

description: Assignment operators are used to assign values to variables. The basic assignment operator is =. C++ also provides compound assignment operators that perform an operation and assignment in a single statement. See 'Compound Assignment Operators' for more information.
syntax: variableName = assignment expression
examples: age = 25;  -- assigns a value to the variable
price = 19.95; * 1.0825;  -- computes the expression, then assigns the value to the variable
string name = "Alice";

description: Compound assignment operators perform an operation on a variable and assign the result back to the same variable. They provide a shorter way to update the current value of a variable.
syntax: variable operator= value;
examples: x += 5;    // equivalent to x = x + 5;
x -= 5;    // equivalent to x = x - 5;
x *= 5;    // equivalent to x = x * 5;
x /= 5;    // equivalent to x = x / 5;
x %= 5;    // equivalent to x = x % 5;

description: Arithmetic operators are used to perform mathematical operations on numeric values. C++ provides operators for addition, subtraction, multiplication, division, and remainder.
syntax:
value operator value;
operand operator operand
examples: x + y    // addition
x - 5    // subtraction
4 * y    // multiplication
x / y    // division
x % 3    // modulus (remainder)

description:
Unary operators are operators that work with only one operand. They can be used to change or indicate the value of a variable or expression.

The ++ (increment) operator increases a variable by 1, while the -- (decrement) operator decreases a variable by 1.

The + (unary plus) operator indicates that a value is positive, while the - (unary minus) operator changes the sign of a value.

The ! (NOT) operator is also a unary operator because it works with one Boolean expression. See Logical operators for more information about the NOT operator.
syntax:
++variable
variable++
--variable
variable--
+value
-value
!condition
examples:
Increment count by 1.
count++;

Decrement count by 1.
count--;

Change a positive value to a negative value.
number = -number;

Use the NOT operator to reverse a Boolean value.
if(!gameOver)

description:
The increment and decrement operators are unary operators used to increase or decrease the value of a variable by 1.

The ++ (increment) operator increases the value of a variable by 1, while the -- (decrement) operator decreases the value of a variable by 1.

The operators can be placed before or after a variable. When used by themselves, prefix and postfix produce the same final value.

When used as part of a larger expression, prefix changes the variable before its value is used, while postfix uses the current value first and then changes the variable.
syntax:
++variable	 prefix increment
variable++	 postfix increment
--variable	 prefix decrement
variable--	 postfix decrement
examples:
Increment count by 1 using postfix increment.
count++;

Decrement count by 1 using postfix decrement.
count--;

description:
Logical operators are used to combine or modify Boolean expressions. The result of a logical operation is either true or false.

The && (AND) operator combines two conditions and is true only when both conditions are true.

The || (OR) operator combines two conditions and is true when at least one of the conditions is true.

The ! (NOT) operator reverses the result of a Boolean expression. A true expression becomes false, and a false expression becomes true.

Logical operators are often used in the conditions/expressions in if and loop structures.
syntax:
condition1 && condition2
condition1 || condition2
!condition
examples:
Use the AND operator to check if age is between 18 and 65.
if(age >= 18 && age <= 65)

Use the OR operator to check if the temperature is outside the normal range.
if(temperature < 60 || temperature > 80)

Use the NOT operator to check if the game is not over.
if(!gameOver)

description:
Comparison operators are used to compare two values. The result of a comparison is a Boolean value of true or false.

The == (equal to) operator checks if two values are equal, while the != (not equal to) operator checks if two values are not equal.

The > (greater than) and < (less than) operators compare whether one value is greater than or less than another value.

The >= (greater than or equal to) and <= (less than or equal to) operators compare values while also allowing them to be equal.
syntax:
value1 == value2
value1 != value2
value1 > value2
value1 < value2
value1 >= value2
value1 <= value2
examples:
Check if age is equal to 18.
if(age == 18)

Check if score is not equal to 0.
if(score != 0)

Check if temperature is greater than 100.
if(temperature > 100)

Check if grade is greater than or equal to 70.
if(grade >= 70)

description:
A Boolean expression is an expression that evaluates to either true or false. Boolean expressions are commonly used to make decisions and control the flow of a program.

Boolean expressions can be created using relational operators to compare values, or logical operators to combine or modify conditions.

A bool variable can also be used as a Boolean expression because its value is already either true or false.
syntax:
value1 relationalOperator value2
condition1 logicalOperator condition2
boolVariable
examples:
Compare age to 18. The expression evaluates to true if age is 18 or greater.
age >= 18

Check if score is between 70 and 100.
score >= 70 && score <= 100

Check if choice is equal to Y or y.
choice == 'Y' || choice == 'y'

description:
An expression is a combination of values, variables, operators, and function calls that can be evaluated to produce a value.

Expressions can perform calculations, compare values, or produce other results that can be assigned to variables, used as conditions, passed to functions, or output.

The data type of an expression depends on the values and operations used in the expression.
syntax:
operand operator operand
variable = expression;
examples:
An arithmetic expression that evaluates to a numeric value.
length * width

Use an expression to calculate and assign a value.
area = length * width;

An expression using several arithmetic operators.
total = price * quantity + shipping;

A Boolean expression that evaluates to true or false.
age >= 18

Use the result of a function call as part of an expression.
total = getPrice() * quantity;

description:
Order of operations determines the order in which operations in an expression are performed. C++ uses operator precedence rules to determine which operations are performed first.

For arithmetic expressions, parentheses are evaluated first, followed  by multiplication, division, and modulus, then addition and subtraction.

Operators with the same precedence are generally evaluated according to their associativity. For example, multiplication and division have the same precedence and are evaluated from left to right.

Parentheses can be used to change the order of operations and can also make complex expressions easier to understand.You can ask for 'Order of Operations Chart' for a detailed chart.
examples:
An arithmetic expression that evaluates to a numeric value.
length * width

Use an expression to calculate and assign a value.
area = length * width;

An expression using several arithmetic operators.
total = price * quantity + shipping;

A Boolean expression that evaluates to true or false.
age >= 18

Use the result of a function call as part of an expression.
total = getPrice() * quantity;

description:
Operator(s)			Description
----------------------------------------------------------------------------------------
()					Parentheses
++, --				Postfix increment/decrement operators
++, __, !, +/-			Prefix/unary operators (not, positive/negative)
*, /, %				Multiplication, division, modulus (left to right)
+, -					Addition, subtraction (left to right)
<, <=, >, >=			Relational (inequality) operators (left to right)
==, !=				Equality operators (left to right)
&&					Logical 'And'
||					Logical 'Or'
=, +=, -=, *=, /=, %=	Assignment operators (right to left)

Type casting is a way of converting one data type to another data typeThere are two types of type casting: implicit and explicit.

With implicit casting the compiler will convert the data type automatically. This can be done when the precision of the value isn't changed: such as 3 converted to 3.00 doesn't change the value.

With explicit casting you, as the programmer, explicitly tell the compiler to convert the data; this is needed when precision can be lost: if 3.14 is changed to 3, precision is lost.

Type casting can be done and assigned to a variable, or used in an output statement.
syntax: static_cast<dataType>(valueToBeConverted)
examples:
Cast the sum of the integers to a float, then divide by 3 to get a flaoting point average.
average = static_cast<float>(98 + 85 + 92) / 3.0;

Same as above but is output instead of assigned to a variable
cout << static_cast<float>(98 + 85 + 92) / 3.0 << endl;

Cast the sum of the variables to a float, then divide by 3 to get a flaoting point average.
average = static_cast<float>(grade1 + grade2 + grade3) / 3.0;

description:
A literal is a value written directly in the source code of a program. Unlike a variable, a literal represents the actual value rather than a named location that stores a value.

Common literals include integer literals, floating-point literals, character literals, string literals, and Boolean literals.

The way a literal is written helps determine its data type. For example, 25 is an integer literal, 25.5 is a floating-point literal, 'A' is a character literal, "Hello" is a string literal, and true is a Boolean literal.
syntax:
Integer:	25
Floating-point:	25.5
Character:	'A'
String:		"Hello"
Boolean:	true or false
examples:
Assign an integer literal to a variable.
int age = 25;

Assign a floating-point literal to a variable.
double price = 19.95;

Assign a character literal to a variable.
char grade = 'A';

Assign a string literal to a variable.
string name = "Alex";

Assign a Boolean literal to a variable.
bool gameOver = false;

description:
A magic number is a numeric value written directly in code without clearly identifying what the value represents. Named constants should be used instead of magic numbers when the value has a specific meaning.

Also one can update the named constant and that 'magic number' is updated throughout the whole program.
Many times the named constant will be declared as a global variable.
examples:
as .0825 might not be readily understood as a tax rate:
const double TAX_RATE = 0.0825;

As 18 may not be understood as the minimum voting age:
const int MIN_VOTING_AGE = 18;

While the number used in the square brackets as an array size is understood, using a named constant helps when you change the size to use the new value throughout the program.
const int ARRAY_SIZE = 100;

description:
A string is a data type used to store a sequence of characters, such as a word, name, sentence, or other text.

A string variable can be declared using the string data type. The <string> header file must be included to use strings.

String literals are enclosed in double quotation marks. Individual characters in a string can be accessed using an index, with the first character at index 0.
examples:
Declare a string variable.
string name;

Declare and initialize a string variable.
string name = "Alex";

Access the first character of a string.
char firstLetter = name[0];

Change an individual character in a string.
name[0] = 'A';

description:
String concatenation is the process of combining two or more strings into a single string.

In C++, strings can be concatenated using the + operator. The += operator can be used to add text to an existing string.

The append() function can also be used to add a string to the end of another string.
examples:
Combine two strings using the + operator.
string fullName = firstName + lastName;

Combine strings with a space between them.
string fullName = firstName + " " + lastName;

Add text to an existing string using +=.
message += " World";

Add text to the end of a string using append().
message.append(" World");

description:
Individual characters in a string can be accessed using their position, called an index.

String indexes begin at 0, so the first character is at index 0, the second character is at index 1, and so on.

Characters can be accessed using the [] operator or the at() function. Both can also be used to change an individual character in a string.

The at() function checks whether the index is within the string, while the [] operator does not perform bounds checking.
syntax:
stringName[index]
stringName.at(index)

description:
String functions are member functions provided by the C++ string class that can be used to examine, search, access, add, remove, or modify the contents of a string.

String functions are called using the string variable followed by the dot operator (.) and the name of the function.

Some commonly used string functions are length(), size(), empty(), at(), substr(), find(), rfind(), compare(), append(), insert(), erase(), replace(), and clear().

See the individual string function topics for descriptions, syntax, and examples of each function.
syntax: stringName.functionName();
examples:
Get the number of characters in a string.
name.length();

Check if a string is empty.
name.empty();

Search for text within a string.
name.find("Alex");

Remove all characters from a string.
name.clear();

description:
The length() function returns the number of characters in a string.

Spaces and other characters are included in the length of the string.

For strings, length() and size() return the same value.

The value is typically returned as an unsigned int.
syntax: stringName.length()

description:
The size() function returns the number of characters in a string.

Spaces and other characters are included in the size of the string.

For strings, size() and length() return the same value.

The value is typically returned as an unsigned int.
syntax: stringName.size()

description:
The empty() function checks whether a string contains no characters.

It returns true if the string is empty and false if the string contains one or more characters.
syntax: stringName.empty()

description:
The at() function accesses a character at a specified index in a string.

String indexes begin at 0, so at(0) accesses the first character.

Unlike the [] operator, at() performs bounds checking and throws an exception if the index is outside the string.

Both the [] operator and at() can be used to read or change a character.
syntax: stringName.at(index)

description:
The substr() function returns part of a string as a new string.

The first argument specifies the starting index and the optional second argument specifies the number of characters to return.

If the number of characters is omitted, substr() returns the characters from the starting index to the end of the string.
syntax:
stringName.substr(startIndex)
stringName.substr(startIndex, length)

description:
The find() function searches a string for a character or substring and returns the index where the first match begins.

If the character or substring is not found, find() returns string::npos.
syntax: stringName.find(value)

description:
The append() function adds characters or another string to the end of an existing string.

It modifies the original string rather than creating a separate string.
syntax: stringName.append(stringToAdd);

description:
The insert() function adds characters or another string at a specified position in an existing string.

The first argument specifies the index where the new text will be inserted.
syntax: stringName.insert(index, stringToInsert);

description:
The erase() function removes characters from a string.

The first argument specifies the starting index and the optional second argument specifies the number of characters to remove.

If the number of characters is omitted, all characters from the starting index to the end are removed.
syntax:
stringName.erase(startIndex);
stringName.erase(startIndex, length);

description:
The replace() function removes characters from a specified part of a string and replaces them with new text.

The first argument specifies the starting index, the second specifies the number of characters to replace, and the third specifies the replacement string.
syntax: stringName.replace(startIndex, length, replacement);

description:
The clear() function removes all characters from a string, leaving the string empty.

After clear() is called, the string still exists and can be assigned or have characters added to it again.
syntax: stringName.clear();

description:
The compare() function compares one string to another string.

It returns 0 if the two strings are equal, a value less than 0 if the first string comes before the second string, and a value greater than 0 if the first string comes after the second string.

The comparison is case-sensitive and compares the numeric values of the characters. For standard ASCII characters, uppercase letters have lower ASCII values than lowercase letters. For example, 'A' has a value of 65 and 'a' has a value of 97.

The strings are compared character by character until a difference is found. The values of the first different characters determine which string comes before the other.
syntax: string1.compare(string2)

description:
The rfind() function searches a string for the last occurrence of a character or substring and returns the index where the match begins.

If the character or substring is not found, rfind() returns string::npos.

Unlike find(), which finds the first occurrence, rfind() can be used to find the last occurrence.
syntax: stringName.rfind(value)

description:
The isdigit() function checks whether a character is a numeric digit from 0 through 9.

The function returns a nonzero value if the character is a digit and 0 if it is not. Because a nonzero value is treated as true and 0 is treated as false, isdigit() can be used directly as the condition of an if statement.

The <cctype> header file must be included to use isdigit().
syntax: isdigit(character)

description:
The to_string() function converts a numeric value to a string.

It can be used to convert integer and floating-point values into text so they can be stored or combined with other strings.

The original numeric value is not changed. Instead, to_string() returns a new string containing the converted value.

The <string> header file must be included to use to_string().
syntax: to_string(numericValue)

description:
The isspace() function checks whether a character is a whitespace character.

Whitespace characters include spaces, tabs, newlines, and certain other characters used for spacing or positioning text.

The function returns a nonzero value if the character is whitespace and 0 if it is not. Because a nonzero value is treated as true and 0 is treated as false, isspace() can be used directly as the condition of an if statement.

The <cctype> header file must be included to use isspace().
syntax: isspace(character)

description:
The toupper() function converts a lowercase letter to its uppercase equivalent.

If the character does not have an uppercase equivalent, it is returned unchanged.

The toupper() function returns an int representing the character value of the uppercase character. For standard ASCII characters, this is the ASCII value of the uppercase character. For example, toupper('a') returns the value 65, which represents 'A'.

When storing the returned value in a char variable, static_cast<char>() can be used to explicitly convert the returned integer value back to a character.

The <cctype> header file must be included to use toupper().
syntax: toupper(character)

description:
The tolower() function converts an uppercase letter to its lowercase equivalent.

If the character does not have a lowercase equivalent, it is returned unchanged.

The tolower() function returns an int representing the character value of the lowercase  character. For standard ASCII characters, this is the ASCII value of the lowercase character. For example, tolower('A') returns the value 97, which represents 'a'.

When storing the returned value in a char variable, static_cast<char>() can be used to explicitly convert the returned integer value back to a character.

The <cctype> header file must be included to use tolower().
syntax: tolower(character)

description:
ASCII (American Standard Code for Information Interchange) is a character encoding system that assigns a numeric value to characters such as letters, digits, punctuation marks, and symbols.

For example, the uppercase letter 'A' has an ASCII value of 65, the lowercase letter 'a' has a value of 97, and the character '0' has a value of 48.

Uppercase letters A through Z have values 65 through 90, lowercase letters a through z have values 97 through 122, and the digits 0 through 9 have values 48 through 57.

Because characters have numeric values, they can be compared and used in arithmetic expressions. The numeric value of a character can be displayed by converting the char to an integer.

For a complete ASCII chart, visit: https://www.ascii-code.com/
syntax:
static_cast<int>(character)
static_cast<char>(asciiValue)

description:
A string constructor can be used to create and initialize a string object.

One form of the string constructor creates a string containing a specified number of copies of a character. For example, string(20, '-') creates a string containing 20 hyphens.

Although this constructor can be useful when the number of characters is determined at runtime, it is not as efficient as a string literal when the number of characters  is known. This being the case it should not be used in my class; use a string literal instead.
syntax: string(count, character)
examples:
Use a string literal when the characters are known in advance.
cout << "--------------------\n";

description:
User output allows a program to display information to the user while the program is running.

In C++, output is commonly displayed on the screen using cout. The << insertion operator is used with cout to send values to the output stream.

Output can include string literals, character literals, numeric values, variables, and expressions. Multiple values can be displayed in a single cout statement by using the insertion operator multiple times.

Escape sequences, endl, and output manipulators can be used to control how the output is displayed.
syntax:
cout << value;
cout << value1 << value2;
examples:
Display a message to the user.
cout << "Hello World";

description:
The cout object is used to send output to the standard output stream, which is normally the screen.

The << insertion operator is used with cout to send values to the output stream. The output can include string literals, character literals, numeric values, variables, and expressions.

Multiple values can be displayed using a single cout statement by using the insertion operator multiple times.

Escape sequences, such as \n, or endl can be used to move the output to a new line.
syntax:
cout << value;
cout << value1 << value2;
examples:
Display a string literal.
cout << "Hello World";

Display the result of an expression.
cout << "Total: " << price * quantity << endl;

description:
Escape sequences are special character combinations used to represent characters that are difficult or impossible to type directly inside a string or character literal.

An escape sequence begins with a backslash (\) followed by another character. The two characters are interpreted as a single special character.

Common escape sequences include \n for a new line, \t for a horizontal tab, \\ for a backslash, \" for a double quotation mark, and \' for a single quotation mark.

Escape sequences can be used inside string and character literals.
syntax:
\n	New line
\t	Horizontal tab
\\	Backslash
\"	Double quotation mark
\'	Single quotation mark

description:
The endl stream manipulator moves the output to the beginning of the next line.

In addition to creating a new line, endl flushes the output stream. Flushing the output stream causes buffered output to be sent to its destination immediately.

The \n escape sequence also creates a new line but does not explicitly flush the output stream. For normal output, \n is commonly used when flushing the output stream is not needed.
syntax: cout << endl;

description:
The output buffer is a temporary area used to hold data before it is sent to an output device, such as the screen or a file.

When a program sends data to an output stream, the data may first be placed in the output buffer. Using a buffer can improve efficiency by allowing multiple pieces of output to be collected and sent together.

Flushing the output buffer causes buffered data to be sent to its destination immediately.

The endl stream manipulator creates a new line and flushes the output stream. The \n escape sequence creates a new line but does not explicitly flush the output stream.

I/O manipulators are used to control how data is displayed or processed by an input or output stream.

Many commonly used manipulators control the appearance of output, such as the number of decimal places displayed, field width, alignment, and fill characters.

Some manipulators, such as fixed, showpoint, left, and right, are inserted directly into the output stream. Other manipulators, such as setw(), setprecision(), and setfill(), are functions that require an argument.

Many formatting manipulators are provided by the <iomanip> header file.
syntax:
cout << manipulator << value;
cout << manipulatorFunction(argument) << value;
examples:
Use a manipulator function to specify a field width.
cout << setw(10) << value;

description:
I/O manipulator functions are stream manipulators that accept one or more arguments to control the formatting of input or output.

Common I/O manipulator functions include setw(), setprecision(), and setfill().

These functions are provided by the <iomanip> header file and are commonly used with cout to control field width, numeric precision, and fill characters.

Many formatting manipulators are provided by the <iomanip> header file.
syntax:
#include <iomanip>

cout << manipulatorFunction(argument) << value;
examples:
Set the field width for a value.
cout << setw(10) << value;

Set the precision of floating-point output.
cout << setprecision(2) << value;

Set the character used to fill unused positions in a field.
cout << setfill('-') << setw(10) << value;

description:
The setw() manipulator function sets the minimum field width for the next value sent to the output stream.

If the value uses fewer characters than the specified width, the remaining positions are filled with the current fill character, which is a space by default.

If the value requires more characters than the specified width, the entire value is still displayed.

Unlike many other output formatting settings, setw() applies only to the next value inserted into the stream.

The <iomanip> header file must be included to use setw().
syntax: cout << setw(width) << value;
examples:
Display a value using a minimum field width of 10.
cout << setw(10) << 25;

description:
The fixed manipulator displays floating-point values using fixed-point notation instead of scientific notation.

When fixed is used with setprecision(), the precision specifies the number of digits displayed after the decimal point.

The fixed setting is persistent, meaning it remains in effect for future floating-point output on that stream until the formatting is changed. Because of this, fixed normally only needs to be set once and should not be repeatedly set inside a loop.
syntax:
cout << fixed << value;
cout << fixed << setprecision(precision) << value;

description:
The setprecision() manipulator function controls the precision used when displaying floating-point values.

By default, setprecision() specifies the total number of significant digits displayed.

When used with fixed, setprecision() specifies the number of digits displayed after the decimal point.

The precision setting is persistent, meaning it remains in effect for future floating-point output on that stream until the precision is changed. Because of this, setprecision() normally only needs to be set once and should not be repeatedly called inside a loop.

The <iomanip> header file must be included to use setprecision().

The default precision is 6 digits.
syntax:
cout << setprecision(precision) << value;
cout << fixed << setprecision(decimalPlaces) << value;

description:
The showpoint manipulator causes floating-point values to display a decimal point and trailing zeros when they would otherwise not be displayed.

This can be useful when output should clearly appear as a floating-point value.

The showpoint setting is persistent, meaning it remains in effect for future floating-point output on that stream until the formatting is changed. Because of this, showpoint normally only needs to be set once and should not be repeatedly set inside a loop.
syntax: cout << showpoint << value;

description:
The setfill() manipulator function changes the character used to fill unused positions in an output field.

The default fill character is a space. setfill() is commonly used with setw() to replace those spaces with another character.

The fill character remains in effect for subsequent formatted output until it is changed.

The <iomanip> header file must be included to use setfill().
syntax: cout << setfill(character) << setw(width) << value;

description:
The left manipulator left-aligns values within their output fields.

When the field width is larger than the value being displayed, the value is placed on the left side of the field and the remaining positions are filled using the current fill character.

By default, output fields are right-aligned. The left manipulator changes the alignment to left justification. The left setting is persistent, meaning it remains in effect until another alignment setting, such as right, is used.
syntax: cout << left << setw(width) << value;
examples:
Left-align a string within a field.
cout << left << setw(15) << "Alex";

description:
The right manipulator right-aligns values within their output fields.

When the field width is larger than the value being displayed, the value is placed on the right side of the field and the remaining positions are filled using the current fill character.

Right alignment is the default alignment for numeric output. The right setting is persistent, meaning it remains in effect until another alignment setting, such as left, is used.
syntax: cout << right << setw(width) << value;
examples:
Right-align a value within a field.
cout << right << setw(10) << 95;

description:
Output formatting is the process of controlling how data is displayed to the user.

Proper output formatting makes program output easier to read, understand, and interpret. Formatting can control the width of a field, the alignment of values, the number of decimal places displayed, the fill character used for padding, and whether a decimal point is always shown.

C++ provides output formatting through I/O manipulators found in the <iomanip> header file. Manipulators can be used to produce neatly aligned columns, format numeric values, and improve the appearance of program output.

Consistently formatted output is especially important when displaying tables, reports, financial data, and other information that should be easy for users to read.

User input allows a program to receive data from the user while the program is running.

In C++, input is commonly read from the keyboard using cin or getline().

The cin object is commonly used to read individual values such as integers, floating-point numbers, characters, and strings without spaces.

The getline() function is used to read an entire line of text, including spaces.

A prompt is commonly displayed before reading input so the user knows what information to enter.

The cin object is used to read input from the standard input stream, which is normally the keyboard.

The >> extraction operator is used with cin to read a value and store it in a variable.

When reading a string with cin, input stops when whitespace is encountered. Because of this, cin is useful for reading individual words or values, while getline() is used when an entire line of text needs to be read.

Multiple values can also be read using a single cin statement.
syntax:
cin >> variable;
cin >> variable1 >> variable2;

description:
The getline() function reads input from an input stream and stores it in a string.

Unlike cin with the >> operator, getline() can read input containing spaces. By default, input continues until a newline character is encountered.

When getline() is used after cin >>, a newline character may still be left in the input buffer. This can cause getline() to read an empty line. The leftover newline should be removed before calling getline(). (See cin.ignore())

getline() can read data from different input streams. In this class, we will use getline() with cin and file input streams.

An optional delimiter can be provided as a third argument. A delimiter is a character that tells getline() where to stop reading. When a delimiter is provided, getline() reads characters until that delimiter is encountered instead of stopping at the newline character.

The delimiter is removed from the input stream but is not stored in the string.
syntax:
getline(inputStream, stringVariable);
getline(inputStream, stringVariable, delimiter);

description:
A delimiter is a character used to separate individual pieces of data.

Common delimiters include commas, spaces, tabs, semicolons, and other characters. For example, a comma is commonly used as the delimiter in a CSV (Comma-Separated Values) file.

When reading data, a delimiter can be used to determine where one piece of data ends and the next begins.

The getline() function can use an optional delimiter to determine where it should stop reading. By default, getline() uses the newline character as the delimiter. A different delimiter can be provided when the data is separated by another character.

When getline() encounters the delimiter, the delimiter is removed from the input stream but is not stored in the string.

The input buffer is a temporary area used to hold data entered by the user before the program reads it.

When the user enters data from the keyboard, the characters are placed in the input buffer. Input operations such as cin >> and getline() then read characters from this buffer.

An input operation may not remove everything from the buffer. For example, cin >> reads the requested value but leaves the newline character created when the user presses Enter in the buffer.

This can cause a problem when getline() is used after cin >>. Since getline() normally stops when it encounters a newline character, it may immediately read the leftover newline and return an empty string.

The cin.ignore() function can be used to remove unwanted characters from the input buffer.

String input is used to read text from an input stream and store it in a string variable.

When reading keyboard input, cin >> can be used to read a single word. It stops reading when whitespace, such as a space, tab, or newline, is encountered.

The getline() function can be used to read an entire line of text, including spaces. For this reason, getline() is commonly used when the input may contain multiple words.

When getline() is used after cin >>, a newline character may remain in the input buffer and should be removed before getline() is called. (See cin.ignore())
syntax:
cin >> stringVariable;
getline(cin, stringVariable);

description:
cin provides several functions that can be used to control and examine input from the input stream.

These functions can be used to read individual characters, remove unwanted characters from the input buffer, examine input without removing it, return a character to the input stream, and check or reset the state of the input stream.

Common cin functions include get(), ignore(), peek(), putback(), fail(), and clear().

See the individual cin function topics for descriptions, syntax, and examples of each function.

The cin.get() function reads a single character from the input stream.

Unlike cin >> with a char variable, cin.get() does not skip whitespace. This means it can read characters such as spaces, tabs, and newline characters.
syntax: cin.get(characterVariable);

description:
The cin.ignore() function removes characters from the input stream without storing them.

It is commonly used to remove a newline character left in the input buffer after using cin >> and before using getline().

By default, cin.ignore() removes one character. Arguments can also be provided to specify the maximum number of characters to remove and a delimiter that tells ignore() when to stop.
syntax:
cin.ignore();
cin.ignore(numberOfCharacters, delimiter);
examples:
Remove one character from the input buffer.
cin.ignore();

Remove characters until a newline is encountered.
cin.ignore(1000, '\n');

description:
The cin.peek() function examines the next character in the input stream without removing it.

Because the character remains in the input stream, it can still be read by the next input operation.
syntax: cin.peek()

description:
The cin.putback() function places a character back into the input stream so it can be read again.

It is typically used after a character has been read and the program determines that the character should be processed by a later input operation.
syntax: cin.putback(character);

description:
The cin.fail() function checks whether an input operation has failed.

An input operation can fail when the data entered cannot be converted to the data type of the variable. For example, entering text when cin is attempting to read an integer will cause the input stream to enter a failure state.

cin.fail() returns true when the stream is in a failure state and false otherwise.
syntax: cin.fail()

description:
The cin.clear() function resets the error state of the input stream after an input operation has failed.

For example, if text is entered when cin expects an integer, cin enters a failure state. Calling cin.clear() resets that state so additional input operations can be performed.

cin.clear() does not remove the invalid characters from the input buffer. cin.ignore() can be used after cin.clear() to remove unwanted input.
syntax: cin.clear();

description:
Testing is the process of executing a program with carefully chosen input to verify that it produces the expected results.

Testing helps identify syntax errors, runtime errors, and logic errors before a program is released or submitted.

Good testing includes using a variety of test cases, including normal input, boundary values, invalid input, and special cases. A program should be tested with more than just the values used while writing the code.

Each test case should have an expected result so the program's actual output can be compared to the correct output.

Testing determines whether a program behaves correctly. If a problem is discovered during testing, debugging is used to locate and correct the error.

Programs should be tested after each major change to ensure that new code has not introduced additional errors.
examples:
Suppose a program calculates the average of three test scores.

Possible test cases:
- Typical values: 80, 90, 100
- All zeros: 0, 0, 0
- Maximum values: 100, 100, 100
- Decimal values (if allowed): 89.5, 91.0, 87.5
- Invalid input: -5 or 125 (if scores must be between 0 and 100)

The program's output should be compared to the expected result for each test case.

description:
Debugging is the process of locating, identifying, and correcting errors in a program.

The first step in debugging is determining the type of error that has occurred. Errors are commonly classified as syntax errors, runtime errors, or logic errors.

A common debugging approach is to test one part of the program at a time rather than making many changes at once. After each change, the program should be tested again to verify that the problem has been corrected.

Useful debugging techniques include reading compiler error messages carefully, tracing the program's execution, displaying the values of variables with temporary output statements, using a debugger, and testing with a variety of input values.

Debugging is an important problem-solving skill. Most programmers spend a significant amount of time debugging and improving existing code rather than writing new code.
examples:
A program is intended to calculate the average of three test scores, but it always displays 0.

One debugging approach might be:
1. Verify that the program compiles successfully.
2. Test the program with known input values.
3. Display the values of variables after each calculation using temporary cout statements.
4. Identify where the incorrect value first appears.
5. Correct the error and test the program again.

description:
A compiler is a program that translates source code written in a programming language, such as C++, into code that the computer can execute.

During compilation, the compiler also checks the source code for problems such as syntax errors and certain type-related errors. If errors are found, the compiler reports them so they can be corrected.

An Integrated Development Environment (IDE) is software that provides tools for developing programs. An IDE typically includes a code editor along with tools for compiling, running, and debugging programs.

The compiler and IDE are not the same thing. The IDE provides the environment and tools used to develop the program, while the compiler performs the translation of the source code.

The C++ development environments supported in this course are Xcode, CLion, and Visual Studio Community. Each provides the tools needed to write, compile, run, and debug C++ programs.

Source code is the human-readable instructions written by a programmer using a programming language such as C++.

C++ source code contains elements such as statements, variables, functions, classes, and other instructions that describe what the program should do.

Source code is written and edited using a text editor or an Integrated Development Environment (IDE). A compiler translates the C++ source code into code that the computer can execute.

C++ source files commonly use the .cpp file extension.

Control structures determine the order in which statements in a program are executed.

The three fundamental control structures are sequence, selection, and iteration.

Sequence structure executes statements one after another in the order in which they appear in the program. Sequence is the default flow of execution and does not require a special C++ statement.

Selection structures allow a program to choose between different paths of execution based on a condition or value. C++ selection structures include the if structure, switch structure, and ternary operator.

Iteration structures repeat a statement or code block. C++ iteration structures include the while loop, do-while loop, and for loop.

Control structures can be combined and nested to create more complex program logic. For example, an if structure can be placed inside a loop, or one loop can be placed inside another.

Control Structures
|
|-- Sequence Structure
|   |-- Statements execute in order
|
|-- Selection Structures
|   |-- If Structure
|   |   |-- Simple if
|   |   |-- if-else
|   |   |-- if-else-if
|   |   |-- Nested if structures
|   |-- Switch Structure
|   |-- Ternary Operator
|
|-- Iteration Structures
    |-- While Loop
    |-- Do-While Loop
    |-- For Loop
    |-- Nested Loops

An if structure is a selection control structure that allows a program to choose between different paths of execution.
