An if structure consists of an if statement, its associated code block, and any optional else if statements and else clause that follow it.

The if statement evaluates a Boolean expression. If the expression evaluates to true, the code block associated with the if statement is executed.

An optional else clause provides an alternative code block that executes when the if condition is false. One or more else if statements can be added when multiple conditions must be evaluated.

C++ commonly uses three forms of the if structure:

- Simple if structure - Executes a code block only when a condition is true.
- if-else structure - Chooses between two alternative code blocks.
- if-else-if structure - Evaluates multiple conditions in order until one is true. The optional final else block executes when none of the conditions are true.

Although a final else clause is optional, it is often considered good programming practice because it provides a default action when none of the preceding conditions evaluate to true. For Professor Raymond's class an else is required after an else-if.

The conditions in an if structure are commonly created using comparison operators, logical operators, Boolean variables, or combinations of these.

Only the first true condition in an if-else-if structure has its associated code block executed. After that block finishes, the program continues with the first statement after the entire if structure.

A nested if structure is an if structure that contains another if structure within one of its code blocks.

Nested if structures are used when a second decision should only be evaluated after a previous condition has been satisfied.

Unlike an if-else-if structure, where conditions are evaluated in sequence until one is true, a nested if structure performs one decision and then, if appropriate, performs another decision inside that branch.

Nested if structures are useful when one condition depends on the result of another. However, excessive nesting can make a program difficult to read and maintain. When possible, keep nesting to a minimum by simplifying the program logic or using an if-else-if structure when appropriate.

A switch structure is a selection control structure that allows a program to choose between multiple paths of execution based on the value of an expression.

A switch structure consists of a switch statement, one or more case labels, an optional default label, and the statements associated with each case.

The expression in the switch statement is evaluated once and compared to each case label. The switch expression must evaluate to an integral type (such as int), a character (char), or an enumeration (enum). Floating-point types, such as float and double, cannot be used because their values may not compare exactly. When a matching case is found, execution begins at that case.

Each case label must contain a unique constant value. Variables and expressions cannot be used as case labels.

A break statement is normally used at the end of each case to exit the switch structure. If a break statement is omitted, execution continues into the next case. This behavior is known as fall-through.

The optional default label is executed when none of the case labels match the value of the switch expression. Although optional, including a default case is considered good programming practice because it provides a default action for unexpected values.

A switch structure is often easier to read than a long if-else-if structure when comparing a single value against many constant values.

The ternary operator is a selection operator that evaluates a Boolean expression and returns one of two values depending on whether the expression is true or false.

The ternary operator is the only C++ operator that requires three operands: a condition, a value returned when the condition is true, and a value returned when the condition is false.

The ternary operator is commonly used as a shorter alternative to a simple if-else structure when assigning a value or displaying one of two possible results.

Because the ternary operator returns a value, it can be used anywhere an expression is valid, such as in an assignment statement, a function call, or an output statement.

Although the ternary operator can make simple decisions more concise, complex expressions are often easier to read when written as an if-else structure.

The ternary operator is best used for simple decisions involving two possible outcomes. If the decision becomes more complex or requires multiple conditions, an if-else structure is usually easier to read and maintain. Although C++ allows nested ternary operators, their use is generally discouraged because they reduce code readability and make programs more difficult to understand and debug.
syntax: condition ? expressionIfTrue : expressionIfFalse
examples:
Assigning a value:

string result = (score >= 70) ? "Passing" : "Not Passing";

Displaying output:

cout << ((age >= 18) ? "Adult" : "Minor") << endl;

description:
File I/O (Input/Output) is the process of reading data from files and writing data to files.

Unlike keyboard input and console output, data stored in a file remains available after the program terminates. Files allow programs to store information for later use.

C++ performs file input and output using file streams provided by the <fstream> header file.

The two file stream classes most commonly used are:
- ifstream - Reads data from a file.
- ofstream - Writes data to a file.

Before a program can read from or write to a file, the file must be opened. When file processing is complete, the file should be closed.

File I/O uses many of the same operators as console input and output. The extraction operator (>>) is commonly used to read formatted data from a file, while the insertion operator (<<) is used to write formatted data to a file.

File I/O is commonly used to store program settings, save user data, read configuration files, process reports, and maintain databases of information.Typical steps when using File I/O:

1. Include the <fstream> header file.
2. Declare an ifstream or ofstream object.
3. Open the file.
4. Read from or write to the file.
5. Close the file.

The ofstream class, provided by the <fstream> header file, is used to write data to a text file.

Before data can be written, the file must be opened. A file may be opened when the ofstream object is created or later by calling the open() member function.

Data is written to the file using the insertion operator (<<), just as data is written to the console using cout.

When file processing is complete, the file should be closed using the close() member function.

If the specified file does not exist, it is typically created automatically. If the file already exists, its previous contents are replaced unless the file is opened in append mode (ios::app).

A common programming practice is to open a file only when it is needed and close it as soon as file processing is complete. Keeping a file open longer than necessary may unnecessarily consume system resources and can make the program more difficult to maintain.

Append mode (ios::app) adds new data to the end of an existing file. Existing data is preserved and is not overwritten.

Programs should verify that a file was opened successfully before attempting to read from or write to it. This can be done by using the file stream as a Boolean expression or by calling the is_open() member function.

For Professor Raymond's Programming 1 course, variables are declared at the beginning of a function. Because of this coding standard, creating the ofstream object first and opening the file later using the open() member function will often be the preferred approach.

The ifstream class, provided by the <fstream> header file, is used to read data from a text file.

Before data can be read, the file must be opened. A file may be opened when the ifstream object is created or later by calling the open() member function.

Data is read from the file using the extraction operator (>>), just as data is read from the keyboard using cin. The getline() function may also be used to read an entire line of text.

When file processing is complete, the file should be closed using the close() member function.

Unlike ofstream, ifstream can only open files that already exist. If the specified file cannot be opened, the program should detect the error and respond appropriately.

A common programming practice is to open a file only when it is needed and close it as soon as file processing is complete. Keeping a file open longer than necessary may unnecessarily consume system resources and can make the program more difficult to maintain.

Programs should verify that a file was opened successfully before attempting to read from or write to it. This can be done by using the file stream as a Boolean expression or by calling the is_open() member function.

For Professor Raymond's Programming 1 course, variables are declared at the beginning of a function. Because of this coding standard, creating the ifstream object first and opening the file later using the open() member function will often be the preferred approach.

A loop is a control structure that allows a program to repeatedly execute a statement or block of statements.

Loops are useful when a task must be performed multiple times. Instead of writing the same statements repeatedly, a loop can control how many times the statements are executed.

C++ provides three primary types of loops:
- while loop - checks its condition before each iteration and continues while the condition is true.
- do-while loop - executes the loop body at least once and checks its condition after each iteration.
- for loop - commonly used when the number of iterations can be controlled with initialization, a condition, and an update.

Loops can be controlled in different ways depending on the problem being solved. Common approaches include counter-controlled, sentinel-controlled, flag-controlled, and EOF-controlled loops.

Each execution of the statements in a loop is called an iteration. The condition that controls a loop must eventually allow the loop to stop unless an infinite loop is intentionally required.

Every loop consists of several components that work together to control repetition. Although the syntax differs between loop structures, these components are present in all loops.

Initialization
Sets the starting value of the loop control variable before the loop begins.

Condition
Determines whether another iteration of the loop should execute. The condition is evaluated as a Boolean expression.

Loop Body
Contains the statements that are repeated each time the loop executes.

Update
Changes the loop control variable so the condition will eventually become false and the loop will terminate.

Termination
Occurs when the loop condition evaluates to false. Program execution then continues with the first statement following the loop.

All loops should be designed so that the update eventually causes the condition to become false. Otherwise, the result is an infinite loop.

For Professor Raymond's class, every loop should clearly demonstrate its loop control components: initialization, condition, loop body, and update. Although C++ allows other loop styles, such as while(true), they are not to be used because they do not explicitly demonstrate how loop repetition is controlled.

Pretest and posttest loops are classified according to when the loop condition is evaluated.

A pretest loop evaluates its condition before the loop body executes. If the condition is false when the loop is first reached, the loop body does not execute. Because of this, a pretest loop may execute zero or more times.

The while loop and for loop are pretest loops because their conditions are evaluated before each iteration.

A posttest loop evaluates its condition after the loop body executes. Because the loop body executes before the condition is checked, a posttest loop always executes at least once.

The do-while loop is a posttest loop because its condition is evaluated after each iteration.

A pretest loop is appropriate when the condition should be checked before any statements are executed. A posttest loop is appropriate when the statements must execute at least once before the condition can be evaluated.

Pretest and Posttest Loops
|
|-- Pretest Loops
|   |-- Condition checked before the loop body
|   |-- May execute zero times
|   |-- while loop
|   |-- for loop
|
|-- Posttest Loops
    |-- Condition checked after the loop body
    |-- Executes at least once
    |-- do-while loop

A for loop is a pretest iteration structure that repeats a block of statements while a Boolean expression remains true.

The for loop combines the three primary loop control components—initialization, condition, and update—into a single loop header.

Initialization executes once before the loop begins. The condition is evaluated before each iteration. If the condition is true, the loop body executes. After the loop body finishes, the update statement executes before the condition is evaluated again.

Because the condition is evaluated before each iteration, a for loop is a pretest loop and may execute zero or more times.

A for loop is commonly used when the number of iterations is known or can be determined before the loop begins. Examples include counting, processing arrays or vectors, and repeating a task a specific number of times.

Although all three loop control components are normally present, any of them may be omitted. However, omitting one or more components often makes the loop more difficult to read and is generally discouraged in this course.

The range-based for loop, also known as the for-each loop, is a pretest iteration structure that automatically visits each element in a container, such as an array or vector.

Unlike a traditional for loop, the for-each loop does not require an initialization, condition, or update expression. Instead, the loop automatically processes each element from the beginning of the container to the end.

The range-based for loop is useful when every element in a collection should be processed and the position (index) of each element is not needed.

The term 'range-based' refers to the range of elements contained in an array, vector, or other container. The loop automatically visits every element in that range.

By default, the loop variable receives a copy of each element. Changes made to the loop variable do not modify the original container.

The data type of the loop variable should match the data type of the elements stored in the container. For example, if a vector stores int values, the loop variable should be declared as an int. If a vector stores Student objects, the loop variable should be declared as a Student.

If the loop variable is declared as a reference, changes made to the loop variable modify the original element stored in the container.

A traditional for loop should be used when the index of each element is needed, when only part of a container should be processed, or when elements must be visited in a specific order.

A while loop is a pretest iteration structure that repeats a code block while a Boolean expression remains true.

Because the condition is evaluated before the loop body executes, a while loop may execute zero or more times. If the condition is false when the loop is first reached, the loop body is skipped.

The initialization of the loop control variable normally occurs before the loop. The condition appears in the while statement, and the update normally occurs within the loop body.

A while loop is commonly used when the number of iterations is not known before the loop begins.

The condition or a value used by the condition must be updated within the loop so that the condition can eventually become false. Otherwise, an infinite loop may occur.

While loops may be controlled using several techniques, including a counter, sentinel value, Boolean flag, or the end-of-file condition of an input file.

For Professor Raymond's class, writing while loops with an explicit Boolean condition that clearly shows when the loop will terminate. Loops written as while(true) are not to be used because they hide the loop's terminating condition.

A counter-controlled while loop repeats a specific number of times by using a counter variable to track the number of completed iterations.

The counter must be initialized before the loop begins, tested in the loop condition, and updated during each iteration.

The counter commonly increases or decreases by one, although another amount may be used.

Counter-controlled while loops are useful when the number of repetitions is known or can be determined before the loop begins.

A for loop is often preferred for counter-controlled repetition because it places the initialization, condition, and update together in one loop header. However, a while loop can perform the same type of repetition.

A sentinel-controlled while loop repeats until a special value, called a sentinel value, is entered or encountered.

The sentinel value indicates that no additional data should be processed. It is not part of the valid data and should not be included in calculations or other processing.

The first value is normally entered before the loop begins. This initial input is called a priming read because it provides the value needed to evaluate the loop condition.

Another input statement is placed near the end of the loop body so that the user can enter the next value. Without this update, the loop condition would continue testing the same value and could create an infinite loop.

The sentinel should be a value that cannot be confused with valid input. For example, -1 may be an appropriate sentinel when all valid values must be zero or greater.

A sentinel-controlled loop differs from a flag-controlled loop because the loop is terminated by a special data value entered or read from the input. No separate Boolean variable is required.

A flag-controlled while loop uses a Boolean variable, called a flag, to determine whether the loop should continue.

A flag variable stores either true or false. It normally represents whether a particular condition or event has occurred, such as whether a value was found, an operation succeeded, or the user chose to stop.

The flag must be initialized before the loop begins. A statement within the loop changes the flag when the event controlling the loop occurs.

Flag variables should have descriptive names such as found, finished, valid, or continueLoop. A descriptive name makes the meaning of the loop condition easier to understand.

If the flag is never changed to the value that terminates the loop, an infinite loop may occur.

A flag-controlled loop differs from a sentinel-controlled loop because the loop is controlled by a separate Boolean variable rather than by the data itself. The flag is updated when a specific event or condition occurs.

An EOF-controlled while loop repeats while data remains available in an input file. EOF stands for end-of-file.

The eof() member function reports whether an attempt has been made to read beyond the end of the file. It does not normally become true immediately after the final valid value or line has been read.

When eof() is used as the loop condition, a priming read should occur before the loop. The data is processed inside the loop, and another read occurs at the end of the loop body.

The read statement inside the loop is the update that moves the file stream toward the end of the file. Omitting this read can cause an infinite loop.

An EOF-controlled loop is useful when the program does not know in advance how many values, records, or lines are stored in the file.

A do-while loop is a posttest iteration structure that repeats a block of statements while a Boolean expression remains true.

Unlike a while loop, the loop condition is evaluated after the loop body executes. Because of this, the loop body always executes at least once.

Variables used by the loop condition are often assigned values within the loop body before the condition is evaluated. Because the loop body executes before the condition is tested, variables do not always need to be initialized before the loop begins.

Like a while loop, a do-while loop may be implemented using several loop control techniques, including counter-controlled, sentinel-controlled, flag-controlled, and EOF-controlled repetition.

A do-while loop is commonly used for menu-driven programs, input validation, and other situations where the statements in the loop must execute before the condition can be evaluated.

Like all loops, the condition or a value used by the condition must eventually change so the condition becomes false. Otherwise, an infinite loop may occur.

A do-while loop differs from a while loop because the loop body executes before the condition is tested. A while loop may execute zero times, whereas a do-while loop always executes at least once.

Notice that the while statement ends with a semicolon. The semicolon is required because it terminates the while statement.

The while statement is written immediately after the closing curly brace of the loop body. This placement is unique to the do-while loop because the condition is evaluated after the statements in the loop body execute.

For Professor Raymond's class, the do-while loop is the only situation in which a statement is intentionally written immediately after a closing curly brace. In all other control structures, statements following a closing curly brace begin on the next line.

An infinite loop is a loop whose terminating condition never becomes false. As a result, the loop continues to execute indefinitely unless the program is stopped or interrupted.

Infinite loops are usually caused by one or more programming errors. Common causes include:
- Forgetting to update the loop control variable.
- Writing an incorrect loop condition.
- Updating the wrong variable.
- Resetting the loop control variable each iteration.
- Using a condition that can never become false.

Every loop should have a clearly defined terminating condition. The statements within the loop should eventually cause that condition to become false.

Infinite loops may occur with any loop structure, including while loops, do-while loops, and for loops.

Although infinite loops are usually programming errors, they are sometimes used intentionally in advanced programs such as operating systems, servers, event-driven applications, and games. These intentional infinite loops normally terminate only when the program is closed or an external event occurs.

Advanced C++ programs sometimes use intentional infinite loops, such as while(true). Those loops are beyond the scope of this course because they do not explicitly demonstrate the loop control components used to construct well-defined loops.

A nested loop is a loop that is contained entirely within another loop. The surrounding loop is called the outer loop, and the loop inside it is called the inner loop.

Each time the outer loop executes one iteration, the inner loop executes all of its iterations before the outer loop continues.

Nested loops are commonly used to process two-dimensional data, create tables and patterns, compare groups of values, and solve problems that require one task to be repeated for every iteration of another task.

The inner loop normally completes all of its iterations before the outer loop is updated and its condition is evaluated again.

Any loop structure may be nested inside another loop. For example, a for loop may contain another for loop, a while loop, or a do-while loop.

Nested Loops
|
|-- Outer Loop
|   |-- Executes one iteration
|   |-- Starts the inner loop
|
|-- Inner Loop
    |-- Completes all iterations
    |-- Returns control to the outer loop

When designing nested loops, choose descriptive loop control variable names. For example, row and column are often more meaningful than i and j when processing rows and columns of data.

The break statement immediately terminates the execution of the nearest enclosing loop or switch structure. Program execution continues with the first statement following the loop or switch.

When used within a loop, break causes the loop to end immediately, even if the loop condition is still true.

When used within a switch structure, break prevents execution from continuing into the next case. For this reason, break is normally used at the end of each case.

For Professor Raymond's class, Although C++ allows break to terminate a loop early, this course does not allow its use within loops. Instead, students should construct loop conditions that clearly describe when the loop should terminate.

The primary exception is the switch structure, where break is normally required to prevent fall-through into the next case.
syntax: break;

description:
The continue statement immediately ends the current iteration of a loop and begins the next iteration.

When a continue statement executes, the remaining statements in the current iteration are skipped. Control returns to the loop condition or update statement, depending on the type of loop.

For Professor Raymond's class, Although C++ provides the continue statement, this course does not allow its use. Instead, programs should be designed so that the loop logic clearly determines which statements execute during each iteration without prematurely skipping the remainder of the loop body.

Avoiding continue encourages the development of clear Boolean expressions and well-structured program logic.
syntax: continue;

description:
Input validation is the process of checking user input to make sure it is acceptable before the program uses it.

Validation helps prevent incorrect calculations, unexpected behavior, and runtime errors caused by invalid data.

A program may validate input by checking:
- Whether a value is within an acceptable range.
- Whether a menu choice matches one of the available options.
- Whether required text was entered.
- Whether a value has the expected data type.
- Whether the input satisfies a specific rule or format.

Input validation is performed before the input is used. The technique used depends on the program. Some programs repeatedly prompt the user until valid input is entered, while others display an error message and continue processing appropriately.

The validation condition should clearly describe which values are invalid. The loop continues while the input is invalid and ends when valid input is received.

Validation should occur as soon as possible after the input is entered and before the value is used in calculations, decisions, or other processing.

Input validation improves the reliability and usability of a program, but it does not guarantee that the user entered truthful or meaningful information. It only verifies that the input follows the rules established by the program.

Range validation checks whether an entered value falls within an acceptable minimum and maximum range.

A value is invalid when it is less than the minimum allowed value or greater than the maximum allowed value. The logical OR operator is commonly used to combine these two invalid conditions.

For example, a test score that must be between 0 and 100 is invalid when it is less than 0 or greater than 100.

A validation loop may repeatedly display an error message and request another value until the user enters a value within the acceptable range.

The minimum and maximum values may be inclusive or exclusive. The comparison operators used in the validation condition must match the rules of the program.

Menu validation handles selections that do not correspond to one of the options provided by a menu.

An invalid menu selection is normally handled by the default case of the switch structure rather than by a separate validation loop.

Each valid menu option is represented by a case label. If the user's selection does not match any case, the default case displays an appropriate error message.

The menu is typically enclosed within the program's main processing loop. After the default case handles an invalid selection, the main loop naturally displays the menu again. An additional validation loop is therefore unnecessary.

This approach keeps the program logic simpler and allows the switch structure to perform its intended purpose of selecting the action associated with the user's menu choice.

Menu validation assumes that the user entered the expected data type. Entering text when an integer is expected causes an input stream error, which is a separate validation issue.

Data validation checks whether data satisfies the rules and requirements established by a program.

Range validation is one form of data validation, but not every validation rule is based on a numeric range.

Data may also be validated by checking:
- Whether a number is positive, negative, even, or odd.
- Whether required text is empty.
- Whether a character matches one of the allowed choices.
- Whether a date or other value follows an expected format.
- Whether related values are logically consistent.

The validation rule should reflect the meaning of the data. For example, an employee's hours worked may be required to be non-negative, while a product quantity may be required to be greater than zero.

Data should be validated before it is stored, used in calculations, or passed to another part of the program.

Data validation determines whether a value follows the program's rules. It cannot determine whether the user intentionally entered false or misleading information.

Input stream validation handles situations in which an input operation fails because the entered data cannot be stored in the requested data type.

For example, if the program attempts to read an integer and the user enters text, cin enters a failed state. The input operation does not assign a valid value to the variable, and additional input operations will also fail until the stream is repaired.

The fail() member function determines whether the previous input operation failed.

The clear() member function clears the stream's error state so that input operations can be attempted again.

The ignore() member function removes the invalid characters that remain in the input buffer. It is commonly used with numeric_limits<streamsize>::max() to discard everything through the next newline character.

Input stream validation differs from range validation. Stream validation checks whether the input could be stored in the requested data type. Range validation checks whether a successfully entered value is acceptable for the program.

Defensive programming is the practice of designing programs to anticipate invalid input, unexpected conditions, and operations that may fail.

A defensive program does not assume that every input, file, calculation, or operation will always succeed. It checks important conditions and responds appropriately when a problem occurs.

Common defensive programming practices include:
- Validating user input before using it.
- Verifying that files opened successfully.
- Checking that an array or vector index is within its valid bounds.
- Preventing division by zero.
- Checking function parameters before processing them.
- Providing a default case in a switch structure.
- Displaying clear and useful error messages.

Defensive programming does not mean adding unnecessary conditions or duplicate logic. Each check should address a realistic problem and should be placed where the program can respond appropriately.

The goal of defensive programming is to make software more reliable, predictable, and easier to test, debug, and maintain.

An iteration is a single execution, or pass, through the body of a loop. Each time the loop body executes, one iteration has been completed.

A loop may execute zero, one, or many iterations depending on the type of loop and whether its condition evaluates to true.

During each iteration, the statements within the loop body execute, the loop control variable is typically updated, and the loop condition is evaluated to determine whether another iteration should occur.

For a while loop and a for loop, the condition is evaluated before each iteration begins. For a do-while loop, the condition is evaluated after each iteration completes.

A loop terminates when its condition becomes false. The number of iterations executed depends on the loop's control components and the data being processed.

The word iteration describes a single repetition of a loop. The process of repeatedly executing statements is called iteration.

A function is a named block of code that performs a specific task. Rather than writing the same statements multiple times, a function allows the code to be written once and called whenever it is needed.

Functions support modular programming by dividing a large program into smaller, more manageable parts. Each function should perform one well-defined task.

A program always begins execution in the main() function. The main() function can call other functions to perform specific tasks, and those functions may call additional functions if necessary.

Functions improve program organization, readability, testing, debugging, maintenance, and code reuse. Changes made to a function are automatically reflected everywhere the function is called.

A function may:
- Receive information through parameters.
- Perform calculations or other processing.
- Return a value to the calling function, or return no value using void.

Functions are declared with function prototypes and implemented with function definitions. A function executes only when it is called.

Every function consists of several components that define what the function is called, what information it receives, what task it performs, and whether it returns a value.

The basic components of a function are:

Function Components
|
|-- Return Type
|-- Function Name
|-- Parameter List
|-- Function Body
\-- Return Statement (when required)

The return type specifies the type of value returned by the function. If the function does not return a value, the return type is void.

The function name identifies the function and is used when calling it.

The parameter list specifies the information the function receives. A function may have zero or more parameters.

The function body contains the statements that perform the task assigned to the function.

A return statement sends a value back to the calling function when the return type is not void. A void function may use a return statement to exit the function early, but it does not return a value.

Together, these components define how a function is declared, called, and executed.

A function signature identifies a function by its name and the types of its parameters.

Function signatures are important because C++ can have multiple functions with the same name when their parameter lists are different. This is called function overloading.

The number, types, and order of the parameters can distinguish one overloaded function from another.

The return type is not used by itself to distinguish overloaded functions. Two functions cannot be overloaded if their only difference is the return type.

Parameter names are also not part of the function signature. The parameter types are what matter when distinguishing overloaded functions.
syntax: functionName(parameterTypes)

description:
The return type specifies the type of value a function returns to the calling function.

If a function does not return a value, its return type is void.

The return type appears at the beginning of both the function prototype and the function definition.

The value returned by the function must match its declared return type.
syntax: returnType functionName(parameterList);
examples:
int calculateSum(int num1, int num2);

Return Type: int

void displayMenu();

Return Type: void

description:
A return value is a value that a function sends back to the statement that called the function.

A function that returns a value has a return type that specifies the type of value the function will return. For example, a function with a return type of int returns an integer value, while a function with a return type of double returns a floating-point value.

The return statement is used to send a value back from the function. The returned value can be stored in a variable, used in an expression, displayed, passed to another function, or used anywhere else a compatible value can be used.

A function can return only one value directly each time it is called. However, that value can be a more complex type, such as a structure, object, or container that contains multiple pieces of data.

A void function does not return a value to the calling statement.

The function name identifies the function. It is used to call the function from another part of the program.

Function names should clearly describe the task the function performs.

Like variable names, function names should follow the rules for valid identifiers.
syntax: returnType functionName(parameterList);

description:
The parameter list specifies the information a function receives from the calling function.

A function may have zero, one, or multiple parameters.

Each parameter includes both a data type and a variable name.

The parameter list appears inside the parentheses following the function name.
syntax: returnType functionName(type parameter, ...);
examples:
void displayMenu();

This function has no parameters.

description:
The function body contains the statements that perform the task assigned to the function.

The function body begins with an opening curly brace and ends with a closing curly brace.

Local variables declared within the function exist only while the function is executing.

Every function definition contains a function body.

A return statement immediately ends the execution of a function.

If the function has a return type other than void, the return statement also returns a value to the calling function.

A void function may use a return statement without a value to exit the function early.However, for Professor Raymond's class a void function should not have a return statement.

The returned value must match the function's declared return type.

A function call is a statement or expression that transfers program control to a function. When a function is called, the program temporarily pauses execution of the calling function, executes the called function, and then returns to the statement immediately following the function call.

If the function requires information, arguments are supplied in the parentheses. Those arguments are assigned to the function's parameters before the function body begins executing.

If the function returns a value, that value may be assigned to a variable, used in an expression, or ignored if appropriate.
examples:
Calling a void function:

displayMenu();

Calling a function that returns a value:

int total = calculateTotal(price, tax);

description:
A parameter is a variable declared in a function's parameter list. Parameters receive values from the calling function when the function is called.

Each parameter has a data type and a variable name. Parameters behave like local variables and exist only while the function is executing.

The number, order, and data types of the parameters should match the arguments supplied by the function call.

Parameters define what information a function needs in order to perform its task.
syntax: returnType functionName(type parameterName);

description:
An argument is a value or expression supplied to a function when it is called. The arguments provide the information the function needs to perform its task.

Each argument is assigned to the corresponding parameter in the order they appear in the function call.

Arguments may be constants, variables, expressions, or the return values of other functions.

The number, order, and data types of the arguments should match the function's parameter list.
syntax: functionName(argument1, argument2);
examples:
calculateArea(length, width);

Arguments:
length
width

calculateArea(5.5, 8.0);

Arguments:
5.5
8.0

calculateArea(side * 2, height + 1);

Arguments:
side * 2
height + 1

description:
Arguments and parameters work together to pass information to a function, but they are not the same thing.

A parameter is a variable declared in a function's parameter list. Parameters receive values when the function is called.

An argument is the value or expression supplied in the function call. Arguments provide the values that are assigned to the parameters.

The number, order, and data types of the arguments should match the function's parameters.

Comparison:

Arguments                          Parameters
--------------------------------------------------------------
Appear in the function call        Declared in the function
Provide values                    Receive values
May be constants, variables,       Are variables
or expressions
Exist in the calling function      Exist in the called function

Remember:
Arguments send information to a function.
Parameters receive that information.

A function prototype is a declaration that tells the compiler a function exists before it is called. The prototype specifies the function's return type, name, and parameter list, but it does not contain the function body.

Function prototypes allow functions to be called before their definitions appear in the program. Without a prototype, the compiler would not know the function's name, return type, or parameters when it encounters the function call.

In this course, function prototypes are placed after the global variables and before the main() function as part of the standard program structure.

Every function definition should have one corresponding prototype. The prototype and the function definition must have the same return type, function name, and parameter list.

A function prototype ends with a semicolon because it is a declaration, not a function definition.

Although function prototypes are not always required in C++, they are required in this course. Understanding function prototypes prepares students for future topics such as header and implementation files, classes and objects, and modular program design. Using prototypes consistently also promotes good program organization and reinforces the standard program structure used throughout this course.

Parameter names are optional in a function prototype because the compiler only needs the data types to verify function calls. If parameter names are included, they do not have to match the names used in the function definition, although the data types, order, and number of parameters must be identical.

For Professor Raymond's class, function prototypes should include only the parameter data types and should not include parameter names. Omitting the parameter names emphasizes that a function prototype declares only the function's interface, while the function definition provides the implementation.
syntax: returnType functionName(parameterList);
examples:
Prototype for a function with no parameters:

void displayMenu();

Prototype for a function with parameters:

double calculateAverage(int total, int count);

description:
The function life cycle describes the compile-time and run-time events associated with declaring, defining, calling, executing, and returning from a function.

The function prototype and function definition are examined by the compiler during compile time. They do not execute. The function's run-time execution begins only when the function is called.

Function Life Cycle

Compile Time
|
|-- Function Prototype
|      Declares the function's return type, name, and parameter types.
|
\-- Function Definition
       Provides the function body that implements the function.

Run Time
|
|-- Function Call
|      Transfers program control to the called function.
|
|-- Arguments Assigned to Parameters
|      Argument values are assigned to the corresponding parameters.
|
|-- Function Executes
|      Statements in the function body execute in sequence.
|
|-- Return Statement
|      Ends the function and returns a value when required.
|
\-- Control Returns to the Calling Function
       Execution resumes where the function call occurred.

Each time a function is called, a new execution of the function begins. Its parameters and local variables are created when the function begins executing and are destroyed when the function ends.

A function may be called multiple times. Each call begins a separate execution of the function with its own parameters and local variables.

A void function is a function that performs a task but does not return a value to the calling function.

The keyword void is used as the function's return type. Because the function does not return a value, its function call is normally written as a separate statement.

Void functions are commonly used to display output, receive input, modify data through reference parameters, save information to a file, or perform another action that does not need to produce a return value.

When the function reaches the end of its body, control automatically returns to the calling function. A void function may also use a return statement without a value to end the function early.

However, for Professor Raymond's class a void function should not have a return statement.

A void function cannot be used where a value is required, such as on the right side of an assignment statement or within a mathematical expression.

A void function performs an action, while a value-returning function produces a value that can be used by the calling function.

A value-returning function performs a task and returns one value to the calling function.

The function's return type specifies the data type of the value that will be returned, such as int, double, char, bool, string, or a user-defined type.

A value-returning function uses a return statement to send a value back to the calling function. The returned value must be compatible with the function's declared return type.

The returned value may be assigned to a variable, displayed, used in an expression, passed as an argument to another function, or used as part of a condition.

When the return statement executes, the function ends immediately and control returns to the location where the function was called.

A value-returning function returns one value directly. Additional results may be provided through reference parameters or by returning a structure or object.

A void function performs an action, while a value-returning function produces a value that can be used by the calling function.

Function overloading allows multiple functions to have the same name, provided their parameter lists are different. The compiler determines which overloaded function to call by comparing the number, order, and data types of the arguments with each function's parameter list.

An overloaded function must differ in at least one of the following ways:
- The number of parameters.
- The data types of the parameters.
- The order of the parameter data types.

Changing only the parameter names does not create a new overloaded function because parameter names are not part of a function's signature.

Changing only the return type does not create a new overloaded function. The compiler does not use the return type to determine which function to call.

Function overloading allows related operations to share a common name while still accepting different types or amounts of information.
examples:
Function calls:

square(5);          // Calls square(int)
square(5.2);        // Calls square(double)
square(4, 7);       // Calls square(int, int)

description:
A default parameter is a function parameter that has a value assigned in the function prototype. The default value is used when the corresponding argument is omitted from the function call.

Default parameters allow a function to be called with fewer arguments than the total number of parameters. The omitted arguments are replaced by their declared default values.

Default values are normally specified in the function prototype and should not be repeated in the function definition.

Parameter names are not required in a function prototype, including when default values are used. For Professor Raymond's class, prototypes should contain parameter data types and default values, but should not contain parameter names.

Default parameters must appear at the end of the parameter list. After one parameter has a default value, every parameter to its right must also have a default value.

Arguments are matched to parameters from left to right. A caller cannot omit an argument in the middle of an argument list while providing an argument that follows it.

Default parameters are useful when a function has a commonly used value but should still allow the caller to provide a different value when needed.

Default parameters can often reduce the need for function overloading. When the only difference between two functions is that one uses a common value for one or more parameters, a single function with default parameters is usually simpler than writing multiple overloaded functions.

Default parameters are appropriate when a function performs the same task using a commonly used value. Function overloading is more appropriate when different parameter lists require different implementations or behaviors.

Pass by value is a parameter-passing method in which the value of an argument is copied into the corresponding parameter.

The parameter is a separate local variable that belongs to the called function. Changes made to the parameter do not affect the original argument in the calling function.

Pass by value is appropriate when the function only needs to use the argument's value and should not modify the original variable.

Because a copy is created, pass by value can require additional memory and processing when large structures or objects are passed. For simple data types such as int, double, char, and bool, this cost is usually small.

In a function prototype, a pass-by-value parameter is written using only its data type. In this course, parameter names are omitted from function prototypes.

Pass by value is the preferred choice when a function only needs to use an argument's value. For small built-in data types such as int, double, char, and bool, copying the value requires very little memory and helps protect the original variable from unintended modification.

Pass by reference is a parameter-passing method in which a reference parameter refers directly to the original argument rather than receiving a copy of its value.

A reference parameter is declared with an ampersand (&) after the data type. Because the parameter refers to the original variable, changes made to the parameter also change the argument in the calling function.

Pass by reference is appropriate when a function needs to modify an argument or return additional results through its parameters.

Pass by reference does not create a separate copy of the argument. This can be more efficient when passing large structures or objects.

Only variables may normally be passed to non-const reference parameters because the function may modify the original value. Constants and temporary expressions cannot be used where a modifiable reference is required.

In a function prototype, the ampersand is required because it is part of the parameter's type. For Professor Raymond's class, parameter names are omitted from function prototypes.

Efficiency Note: Although pass by reference is often described as being more efficient, this is primarily true for large objects such as vectors, structures, and classes. For small built-in data types such as int, char, bool, and even double, the performance benefit is typically negligible. In many cases, the reference itself occupies as much or more memory than the value being passed. In this course, choose pass by reference because the function needs to modify the caller's variable or avoid copying a large object—not simply because it is assumed to be faster.

Modular programming is the practice of dividing a program into smaller, independent parts called modules. In a C++ program, functions are commonly used as modules.

Each module should perform one specific, well-defined task. For example, separate functions may be used to display a menu, receive input, perform calculations, validate data, save information to a file, or display results.

Breaking a large problem into smaller tasks is called program decomposition. Each task can then be designed, written, tested, and debugged separately before being combined into the complete program.

Modular programming improves:
- Organization, because related statements are grouped together.
- Readability, because each function has a clear purpose.
- Testing and debugging, because individual functions can be examined separately.
- Maintenance, because changes can often be made within one function.
- Code reuse, because a function can be called whenever its task is needed.

A well-designed function should normally perform one primary task. If a function performs many unrelated tasks, it may need to be divided into smaller functions.

The main() function should provide the overall flow of the program and call other functions to perform the detailed tasks. Placing most of the program's work in appropriately named functions makes main() easier to read and understand.

As programs become larger, modular design may also use header files, implementation files, structures, classes, and objects to organize related data and behavior.

keywords: Where a variable can be used
description:
Scope defines where a variable can be accessed within a program. A variable may only be used within the region of the program in which it is visible.

The most common types of scope are:

Scope
|
|-- Global Scope
|      Variables declared outside all functions.
|      Accessible throughout the program.
|
|-- Local Scope
|      Parameters and variables declared within a function.
|      Accessible only within that function.
|
\-- Block Scope
       Variables declared inside a pair of curly braces ({ }).
       Accessible only within that block.

A variable becomes visible when its declaration is encountered and remains visible until the end of its scope.

When a variable goes out of scope, it no longer exists and cannot be accessed.

Variables with the same name may exist in different scopes. A variable declared in an inner scope hides, or shadows, a variable with the same name declared in an outer scope.

Limiting a variable's scope helps prevent accidental modification, reduces naming conflicts, and makes programs easier to understand and maintain.

Whenever possible, declare a variable in the smallest scope in which it is needed. Limiting a variable's scope reduces the chance of unintended modifications and makes programs easier to read and maintain.

However, for Professor Raymond's class variables should be declared at the top of the function and global variables should only be used when explicitly authorized. You should not be using bock scope variables.
syntax: There is no  syntax for scope.

description:
A global variable is declared outside all functions. It has global scope, meaning it can be accessed by every function in the program after its declaration.

Global variables exist for the entire execution of the program.

Although global variables are useful in some situations, overusing them can make programs more difficult to understand, test, and maintain because many functions can modify the same variable.

In general, variables should be declared in the smallest scope in which they are needed. Global variables should be used only when multiple functions must share the same data.

For Professor Raymond's class you should only use global variables when specifically authorized. If you think a global variable is needed, you can ask for authorization to  use one.
syntax:
dataType variableName;

Declared outside all functions.

description:
A local variable is declared within a function. It can be accessed only within that function.

Local variables are created when the function begins executing and are destroyed when the function ends.

Parameters are also local variables because they exist only while the function is executing.

Local variables with the same name may exist in different functions because each function has its own scope.

Whenever possible, variables should be declared as local variables instead of global variables because they reduce unintended interactions between functions.
syntax:
dataType variableName;

Declared inside a function.

description:
Block scope is the region of a program enclosed by a pair of curly braces ({ }). Variables declared within a block are accessible only inside that block.

Blocks are created by statements such as if, else, switch, for, while, do-while, and functions.

A variable declared within a block is destroyed when execution leaves that block.

Variables declared within a block may hide variables with the same name declared in an outer scope. This is known as variable shadowing.

Block scope allows temporary variables to exist only where they are needed, reducing the possibility of accidental misuse elsewhere in the program.

for Professor Raymond's class you should not use block scope variables, all variables should be declared at the top of the function (local scope). There is one exception, the loop control variable in a for loop can be declared when initializing the loop control variable.

An instance variable is a variable declared within a class. Each object created from the class has its own separate copy of every instance variable.

Instance variables store the data that describes the state of an object.

When a new object is created, memory is allocated for its instance variables. Different objects of the same class store their own independent values.

Instance variables are typically accessed through an object using the dot (.) operator.

Instance variables are declared in the class specification file (.hpp or .h). Keeping the instance variables in the class specification clearly defines the data that every object contains, while the member function implementations are placed in the corresponding implementation (.cpp) file.

A user-defined header file is a file that contains declarations shared by one or more source files. Header files are commonly used to declare constants, structures, classes, function prototypes, enumerations, namespaces, and other information that multiple source files need to access.

Header files define what a program component contains and what it can do, but they do not normally contain the implementation of functions.

Separating declarations from implementations supports abstraction by allowing other parts of the program to use a class or function without knowing how it is implemented.

Course Coding Standard: In this course, user-defined header files contain declarations only. Function definitions should be placed in the corresponding implementation (.cpp) file.

Header files are included in source files using the #include preprocessor directive.
syntax:
#ifndef HEADER_NAME_HPP
#define HEADER_NAME_HPP

// declarations

#endif

description:
An implementation file (.cpp) contains the executable code that implements the functions or member functions declared in a user-defined header file.

Implementation files define how a function or class performs its task. They contain the function bodies but typically do not repeat declarations that already appear in the header file.

Separating the implementation from the header file supports abstraction by hiding the implementation details from other source files.

Course Coding Standard: In this course, all function definitions and member function definitions are placed in implementation (.cpp) files. The corresponding header (.hpp or .h) file contains only the declarations.

An implementation file includes its corresponding header file using #include.

Include guards prevent a header file from being included more than once during compilation. Without include guards, the compiler may process the same declarations multiple times, resulting in compilation errors such as duplicate definitions.

The traditional method uses the preprocessor directives #ifndef, #define, and #endif. The first time the header file is included, the guard macro is defined and the file is processed. Any later attempts to include the same header file are skipped.

Many modern C++ compilers also support #pragma once, which provides the same protection using a single preprocessor directive. Although #pragma once is widely supported, it is not part of the C++ language standard.
syntax:
Traditional Include Guard:

#ifndef HEADER_NAME_HPP
#define HEADER_NAME_HPP

// declarations

#endif

Using #pragma once:

#pragma once

// declarations

description:
Pseudo-random numbers are values generated by a mathematical algorithm that appear to be random. They are called pseudo-random because they are generated by a predictable process rather than by a truly random event.

The random number generator produces a long sequence of numbers. Each call to rand() returns the next number in that sequence.

The sequence can be thought of as a very long list of numbers, although the numbers are actually calculated by an algorithm rather than stored in a list.

If the generator begins with the same seed, it produces the same sequence. Changing the seed causes the generator to begin with a different sequence of values.

The values returned directly by rand() may be very large. The modulo operator is commonly used to reduce those values to a smaller range.

For example, rand() % 10 produces values from 0 through 9 because the remainder after division by 10 can only be 0 through 9.
examples:
Limiting a pseudo-random number with the modulo operator:

rand() % 10

Possible results:
0, 1, 2, 3, 4, 5, 6, 7, 8, or 9

Another modulo range:

rand() % 6

Possible results:
0, 1, 2, 3, 4, or 5

description:
The rand() function generates and returns the next pseudo-random integer in the random number generator's sequence.

The rand() function is provided by the <cstdlib> header file.

The value returned by rand() is between 0 and RAND_MAX. Because this range is usually much larger than the range needed by a program, the modulo operator is commonly used to limit the result.

The expression rand() % n generates a value from 0 through n - 1.

For example:
rand() % 10 produces 0 through 9.
rand() % 6 produces 0 through 5.

To generate a value within a specific inclusive range, use:

(rand() % (upperBound - lowerBound + 1)) + lowerBound

The expression upperBound - lowerBound + 1 calculates the number of possible values in the desired range. The modulo operator produces a value starting at zero, and adding lowerBound shifts the result into the requested range.
syntax:
Generate an unrestricted pseudo-random integer:

rand()

Generate a value from 0 through n - 1:

rand() % n

Generate a value from lowerBound through upperBound:

(rand() % (upperBound - lowerBound + 1)) + lowerBound
examples:
Generate a value from 0 through 9:

int number = rand() % 10;

Generate a value from 1 through 10:

int number = (rand() % 10) + 1;

Generate a value from 50 through 100:

int number = (rand() % (100 - 50 + 1)) + 50;

The expression 100 - 50 + 1 produces 51 possible values.
The modulo operation produces 0 through 50.
Adding 50 shifts the range to 50 through 100.

Generate a value from 256 through 4095:

int number = (rand() % (4095 - 256 + 1)) + 256;

description:
Seeding the random number generator initializes the sequence of pseudo-random numbers produced by rand(). In C++, the srand() function supplies the seed used by the random number generation algorithm.

The seed determines the sequence of values returned by later calls to rand(). Using the same seed produces the same sequence of pseudo-random numbers. This can be useful during testing and debugging because the results can be reproduced.

Using a different seed normally produces a different sequence. Programs commonly use the current time as the seed because the time normally changes between program executions.

The time() function returns a value with the data type time_t. The time_t type is defined by the <ctime> header file and is used to represent calendar time. Its exact underlying data type is determined by the system.

On most systems, time() returns the number of seconds that have elapsed since January 1, 1970 at 00:00:00 UTC. This starting point is commonly called the Unix epoch.

The expression time(nullptr) requests the current calendar time. The nullptr argument indicates that the returned time should not also be stored through a pointer.

The srand() function accepts an unsigned int seed. Because time() returns a time_t value, the returned value may be explicitly converted to unsigned int before it is passed to srand().

The seed does not directly become the first random number. Instead, it initializes the algorithm that generates the sequence.

The random number generator should normally be seeded only once near the beginning of main(), before the first call to rand(). It should not be reseeded each time a random number is needed.

Repeatedly calling srand() within a loop can cause repeated or less varied results, especially when several calls receive the same time value.

Preprocessor directives are special instructions that are processed before the C++ compiler begins compiling a program. They allow the preprocessor to prepare the source code by including files, defining constants, and controlling which portions of code are compiled.

Preprocessor directives begin with the # (number sign) character. Unlike C++ statements, they are not executed while the program is running. Instead, they are processed before compilation begins.

Common preprocessor directives include:

Preprocessor Directives
|
|-- #include
|      Includes another file.
|
|-- #define
|      Defines a preprocessor macro.
|
|-- #ifndef / #endif
|      Prevents multiple inclusion of header files.
|
\-- #pragma once
       Modern alternative to traditional include guards.

Preprocessor directives are handled before compilation. After preprocessing is complete, the compiler receives the modified source code for compilation.

Although preprocessor macros can define constants, this course uses constexpr and const variables instead because they provide type safety, better compiler checking, and improved debugging support.
syntax:
General form:

#directive arguments

Examples:
#include <iostream>
#include "Student.hpp"
#define PI 3.14159
#ifndef STUDENT_HPP
#define STUDENT_HPP
#endif
#pragma once
examples:
Include a standard library header:

#include <iostream>

Include a user-defined header:

#include "Student.hpp"

description:
An array is a collection of multiple values of the same data type stored under a single variable name.

Each value stored in an array is called an element. Individual elements are accessed using an index, which represents the element's position within the array.

C++ arrays use zero-based indexing. This means that the first element has an index of 0, the second element has an index of 1, and so on. An array containing n elements has valid indexes from 0 through n - 1.

For example, an array containing five elements can be visualized as:

Index:      0      1      2      3      4
          +------+------+------+------+------+
Element:  |  85  |  92  |  78  |  96  |  88  |
          +------+------+------+------+------+

All elements in an array must have the same data type. For example, an int array stores only integers, while a double array stores only double values.

The size of a traditional C++ array is established when the array is declared and cannot be changed while the program is running.

Arrays are useful when a program needs to store and process a group of related values, such as test scores, temperatures, prices, or other collections of data.

Loops are commonly used with arrays because the index can be changed during each iteration to process each element in sequence.

Unlike a single variable, which stores one value, an array allows many related values to be stored and accessed using one variable name and different indexes.

An array has several components that determine what it stores and how its elements are accessed.

Array Components
|
|-- Data Type
|      Determines the type of value that each element can store.
|
|-- Array Name
|      Identifies the array and is used to access its elements.
|
|-- Array Size
|      Determines the number of elements the array can contain.
|
|-- Elements
|      The individual values stored in the array.
|
\-- Index
       Identifies the position of an individual element in the array.

For example, in the declaration int scores[5], int is the data type, scores is the array name, and 5 is the array size. The array contains five elements with indexes from 0 through 4.

The data type applies to every element in the array. A traditional C++ array cannot contain elements of different data types.

The array size represents the number of elements, not the highest valid index. Because array indexes begin at 0, the highest valid index is always one less than the array size.
syntax: dataType arrayName[arraySize];
examples:
Identify the components of an integer array:

int scores[5];

Data Type: int
Array Name: scores
Array Size: 5
Number of Elements: 5
Valid Indexes: 0 through 4

Identify the components of a double array:

double temperatures[7];

Data Type: double
Array Name: temperatures
Array Size: 7
Number of Elements: 7
Valid Indexes: 0 through 6

description:
An array must be declared before it can be used. An array declaration specifies the data type of its elements, the array name, and the number of elements the array can contain.

An array may be declared without assigning initial values to its elements, or it may be initialized when it is declared by providing values inside curly braces ({ }).

When an array is initialized, the values are assigned to the elements in order. The first value is stored at index 0, the second value at index 1, and so on.

If an initializer list contains fewer values than the declared size of the array, the remaining elements are initialized to zero.

When an array is initialized with an initializer list, the array size may be omitted. C++ determines the size from the number of values in the initializer list.

The size of a traditional C++ array is fixed when the array is created and cannot be changed while the program is running.
examples:
Declare and initialize an array:

int scores[5] = {85, 92, 78, 96, 88};

scores[0] contains 85.
scores[1] contains 92.
scores[2] contains 78.
scores[3] contains 96.
scores[4] contains 88.

Provide fewer initial values than the array size:

int scores[5] = {85, 92};

The array contains:
85, 92, 0, 0, 0

Initialize every element to zero:

int scores[5] = {};

The array contains:
0, 0, 0, 0, 0

description:
Individual elements of an array are accessed by placing an index inside square brackets ([ ]) after the array name.

The index identifies which element of the array is being accessed. Because C++ arrays use zero-based indexing, the first element is at index 0, the second element is at index 1, and so on.

An individual array element behaves much like a regular variable. Once an element is selected using its index, its value can be assigned, displayed, used in an expression, compared, or changed.

For example, scores[2] refers to the third element of the scores array.

The index may also be stored in a variable or calculated using an expression. This is what allows loops to process different elements of an array during each iteration.

The index used to access an element must be within the valid range of the array. Accessing an element outside this range is called accessing the array out of bounds. See Array Bounds for more information.

Array traversal is the process of accessing and processing the elements of an array, usually from the first element to the last.

A for loop is commonly used to traverse an array because the loop control variable can also be used as the array index. The loop begins with an index of 0 and continues while the index is less than the size of the array.

For an array containing n elements, the valid indexes are 0 through n - 1. Therefore, the loop condition should normally use index < arraySize rather than index <= arraySize.

During each iteration, the index changes and allows the program to access a different element of the array.

Array traversal can be used to display elements, receive input, modify values, calculate totals or averages, search for values, count values that meet a condition, and perform many other operations on the elements of an array.

Although a while loop can also be used to traverse an array, a for loop is typically preferred when processing every element because the initialization, condition, and update of the index are contained in one statement.

A range-based for loop may also be used to traverse an array when the program needs to process each element and does not need to know the element's index. A range-based for loop accesses the elements directly rather than using an index. See Range-Based :For Loop for more information.

A multidimensional array is an array that uses more than one index to organize and access its elements. The most common type is a two-dimensional array, which organizes elements into rows and columns.

A two-dimensional array can be visualized as a table. The first index identifies the row, and the second index identifies the column.

For example, scores[1][2] accesses the element located at row 1, column 2.

Like a one-dimensional array, indexing begins at 0. Therefore, an array with 3 rows and 4 columns has row indexes 0 through 2 and column indexes 0 through 3.

A two-dimensional array with 3 rows and 4 columns can be visualized as:

              Column
             0    1    2    3
          +----+----+----+----+
Row 0     | 10 | 20 | 30 | 40 |
          +----+----+----+----+
Row 1     | 50 | 60 | 70 | 80 |
          +----+----+----+----+
Row 2     | 90 |100 |110 |120 |
          +----+----+----+----+

Multidimensional arrays are useful for data that naturally forms rows and columns, such as tables, grids, seating charts, game boards, monthly sales by location, or grades for multiple students and assignments.

Nested loops are commonly used to traverse a two-dimensional array. The outer loop typically controls the row, while the inner loop controls the column.

C++ supports arrays with more than two dimensions, but two-dimensional arrays are the most commonly used multidimensional arrays in introductory programs.
examples:
Declare a two-dimensional array with 3 rows and 4 columns:

int scores[3][4];

The array contains 12 total elements.
Valid row indexes are 0 through 2.
Valid column indexes are 0 through 3.

description:
Parallel arrays are two or more arrays that store related data. The arrays use the same index to associate elements with each other.

Each array stores a different type or category of information, but elements at the same index represent information about the same item.

For example, one array might store student names while another stores student grades. names[0] and grades[0] contain information about the same student, names[1] and grades[1] contain information about the next student, and so on.

Parallel arrays can be visualized as:

Index:       0          1          2          3
           ----------------------------------------
Names:     Alex       Jordan      Taylor      Morgan
Grades:      92          85          97          88

The relationship between the arrays depends on maintaining the same indexes. If elements are moved, sorted, inserted, or otherwise changed in one array, the corresponding elements in the other parallel arrays must also be changed so that the relationships remain correct.

Parallel arrays should normally have the same size because each index represents one complete set of related information.

A single loop can process multiple parallel arrays by using the same loop control variable as the index for each array.

Parallel arrays are useful for introducing the idea of storing related data. As programs become more complex, structures and classes provide a better way to group related values into a single object.

keywords: Pass an array to a function
description:
An array can be passed to a function by using the array name as an argument. The function receives access to the original array rather than receiving a complete copy of the array.

When an array is used as a function parameter, empty square brackets ([ ]) are placed after the parameter name to indicate that the parameter represents an array.

The array name is used as the argument in the function call. Square brackets are not included when passing the entire array to the function.

Because the function has access to the original array, changes made to array elements inside the function also change the elements of the original array.

Unlike a regular variable, an array does not automatically provide its size to the function. The number of elements that should be processed is therefore commonly passed as a separate parameter.

The array parameter and the size parameter work together. The array parameter provides access to the elements, while the size tells the function how many elements it should process.

Copying an array creates a copy of the elements from one array in another array. Traditional C++ arrays cannot be copied by assigning one array to another using the assignment operator (=).

For example, destination = source is not valid for copying traditional C++ arrays.

There are several ways to copy the elements of an array. In this course, arrays are copied using an element-by-element for loop, the copy() function, or the copy_n() function.

An element-by-element copy uses a loop to assign each element of the source array to the corresponding element of the destination array. The same index is used with both arrays.

The copy() function copies a range of elements. It requires the beginning of the source range, the location immediately after the end of the source range, and the beginning of the destination array.

With an array, the source range can be identified using begin() and end(), or by using the array name and the + operator. For example, source + size identifies the location immediately after the last element that should be copied.

The copy_n() function copies a specified number of elements. It requires the beginning of the source array, the number of elements to copy, and the beginning of the destination array.

Both copy() and copy_n() are provided by the <algorithm> header file.

The destination array must have enough space to contain all of the elements being copied.

Indexing is the use of a numeric position to access an individual element in a collection of data, such as an array, vector, or string.

C++ uses zero-based indexing, which means the first element is at index 0, the second element is at index 1, and so on.

For a collection containing size elements, the last valid index is size - 1. For example, a collection containing 5 elements has indexes 0 through 4.

An index can be a literal integer, a variable, or an integer expression that evaluates to a valid position.

Attempting to access an index outside the valid range can result in incorrect behavior or a run-time error, depending on how the element is accessed.
