syntax: collectionName[index]
examples:
Access elements of an array using indexes:
int scores[5] = {90, 85, 78, 92, 88};

cout << scores[0];   // first element
cout << scores[4];   // last element

description:
A linear search is a searching algorithm that examines the elements of an array one at a time until the desired value is found or every element has been checked.

The search normally begins at index 0 and moves sequentially through the array. Each element is compared with the value being searched for.

A linear search does not require the array to be sorted. Because every element may need to be examined, a linear search is generally less efficient than a binary search for large amounts of sorted data.

If the value is found, the search can save the index where the value was located. If the entire array is searched without finding the value, a value such as -1 can be used to indicate that the value was not found.

Linear Search

Target: 78

Index:     0    1    2    3    4
Array:    85   92   78   96   88
           |    |    |
           v    v    v
          No   No   Found

The worst-case number of comparisons is equal to the number of elements in the array.

A binary search is a searching algorithm that repeatedly divides the portion of an array being searched in half.

A binary search requires the array to be sorted before the search begins. Without sorted data, the algorithm cannot determine which half of the array can be eliminated.

The search keeps track of the first and last indexes of the portion of the array that may contain the desired value. The middle index is calculated and the middle element is compared with the search value.

If the middle element equals the search value, the value has been found. If the search value is smaller than the middle element, the upper half of the search range is eliminated. If the search value is larger than the middle element, the lower half is eliminated.

This process continues until the value is found or there are no elements remaining in the search range.

Binary Search

Sorted Array:

Index:     0    1    2    3    4    5    6
Array:    10   20   30   40   50   60   70
                          ^
                        Middle

If the target is 60, values at and below 40 can be eliminated because 60 is larger than the middle value.

Because approximately half of the remaining elements are eliminated after each comparison, a binary search is generally much more efficient than a linear search for large amounts of large amounts of sorted data.

The C++ Standard Library provides functions that can search collections of data without requiring the programmer to write the complete searching algorithm.

The std::find() and std::binary_search() functions are provided by the <algorithm> header file.

std::find() performs a linear search through a specified range. It examines elements from the beginning of the range until the requested value is found or the end of the range is reached. The data does not need to be sorted before using std::find().

std::find() returns the location of the matching element. If the value is not found, it returns the end of the search range. When begin() and end() are used, the result can be compared with end(arrayName) to determine whether the value was found.

std::binary_search() performs a binary search and requires the data to already be sorted. It returns true if the requested value is found and false if the value is not found.

Unlike std::find(), std::binary_search() does not return the location or index of the matching element. It only determines whether the value exists within the specified range.

Both functions require a beginning and ending location for the range being searched. The ending location represents the position immediately after the last element to search.

For traditional arrays, begin() and end() may be used to identify the entire array. The array name and + operator may also be used, such as numbers and numbers + size.

These functions provide convenient alternatives to manually implementing searching algorithms. Understanding linear and binary search is still important because it explains how the searches work and why a binary search requires sorted data.

For Professor Raymond's class the use of find() and binary_search() are not authorized.

Sorting an array is the process of arranging its elements into a specified order.

Numeric data is commonly sorted into ascending order, from smallest to largest, or descending order, from largest to smallest. String data can also be sorted alphabetically.

Sorting data can make it easier to display, organize, search, and analyze. Some algorithms, such as binary search, require the data to be sorted before the algorithm can be used.

There are many different sorting algorithms. In this course, bubble sort and selection sort are used to demonstrate how sorting algorithms work.

Bubble sort repeatedly compares adjacent elements and swaps them when they are out of order. Selection sort repeatedly finds the smallest remaining element and moves it into its correct position.

The C++ Standard Library also provides the sort() function, which can sort a range of elements without requiring the programmer to write the sorting algorithm.

Although library functions are normally preferred when writing programs, understanding sorting algorithms such as bubble sort and selection sort helps develop an understanding of algorithms, comparisons, swapping values, nested loops, and efficiency.

Bubble sort is a sorting algorithm that repeatedly compares adjacent elements and swaps them when they are in the wrong order.

To sort an array into ascending order, the algorithm begins by comparing the first two elements. If the first element is greater than the second, the two elements are swapped. The algorithm then moves to the next pair of adjacent elements and continues through the array.

After the first pass through the array, the largest value has moved to the last position. Because that value is now in its correct position, the next pass does not need to compare it.

Each pass places another value into its correct position at the end of the array. The number of comparisons therefore decreases with each pass.

Bubble sort uses nested loops. The outer loop controls the number of passes, while the inner loop compares adjacent elements during each pass.

Bubble sort is relatively easy to understand and implement, which makes it useful for learning how sorting algorithms work. However, it is generally inefficient for large amounts of data compared with more advanced sorting algorithms.

Selection sort is a sorting algorithm that repeatedly finds the smallest value in the unsorted portion of an array and places it into its correct position.

To sort an array into ascending order, the algorithm begins at index 0 and searches the remaining elements for the smallest value. The smallest value is then swapped with the value at index 0.

The algorithm then moves to index 1 and searches the remaining unsorted elements for the next smallest value. This process continues until the array is sorted.

Selection sort uses nested loops. The outer loop identifies the position where the next smallest value should be placed. The inner loop searches the remaining unsorted portion of the array for that value.

Unlike bubble sort, selection sort does not repeatedly swap adjacent elements. Instead, Instead, it remembers the index of the smallest value found during a pass and performs a swap after the search for that pass is complete.

Selection sort is useful for demonstrating searching, comparisons, indexes, nested loops, and swapping values. Like bubble sort, it is generally inefficient for large amounts of data.

The sort() function is a C++ Standard Library function that arranges the elements within a specified range into sorted order.

The sort() function is provided by the <algorithm> header file.

By default, sort() arranges values into ascending order. Numeric values are arranged from smallest to largest, and strings are arranged according to their comparison order.

The function requires the beginning and ending locations of the range to sort. The ending location represents the position immediately after the last element in the range.

For a traditional array, begin() and end() can be used to identify the entire array. The array name and + operator can also be used. For example, numbers + size identifies the location immediately after the last element of the array.

The sort() function changes the order of the elements in the original array. It does not create a separate sorted copy.

Although sort() is normally preferred over manually writing a sorting algorithm, understanding algorithms such as bubble sort and selection sort helps explain the logic and operations involved in sorting data.

For Professor Raymond's class you are not authorized to use the sort() function.

A vector is a C++ Standard Library container that stores a collection of values of the same data type.

Vectors are similar to arrays because their elements are stored in sequence and are accessed using indexes beginning at 0.

Unlike a traditional array, however, a vector can change its number of elements while the program is running. Elements can be added or removed as needed.

A vector keeps track of its own size. The size() function returns the number of elements currently stored in the vector.

Vectors also maintain a capacity, which represents the amount of storage currently available before additional memory must be allocated. The capacity may be greater than the vector's size.

For example, a vector containing five values can be visualized as:

Index:      0      1      2      3      4
          +------+------+------+------+------+
Element:  |  85  |  92  |  78  |  96  |  88  |
          +------+------+------+------+------+

Vectors provide member functions that make many common operations easier, including adding elements, removing elements, checking the number of elements, and managing storage.

Some of the common functions used with vectors can be organized by their purpose:

Vector Size and Resizing
├── size()          → reports number of elements
├── resize()        → changes number of elements
└── clear()         → removes all elements

Vector Capacity and Reserving
├── capacity()      → reports current capacity
├── reserve()       → requests additional capacity
└── shrink_to_fit() → requests reduction of unused capacity

Adding and Removing Vector Elements
├── push_back()     → adds an element to the end
├── pop_back()      → removes the last element
├── insert()        → adds an element at a specified position
└── erase()         → removes an element at a specified position

Vectors are provided by the <vector> header file.

A vector declaration contains several components that describe the vector and the type of data it stores.

The vector type identifies the container as a vector. The data type inside the angle brackets specifies the type of elements the vector can store, and the vector name identifies the vector in the program.

A vector can be declared empty, given an initial size, or initialized with values. Unlike an array, a vector can change its size while the program is running.

Individual elements of a vector can be accessed using an index. Like arrays, vector indexes begin at 0, so the first element is at index 0 and the last element is at index size() - 1.
examples:
Declare an empty vector of integers:
vector<int> scores;

Declare a vector with an initial size of 5:
vector<int> scores(5);

Declare and initialize a vector with values:
vector<int> scores = {85, 92, 78, 96, 88};

Identify the components of a vector declaration:
vector<double> prices;

vector        → vector type
double        → element data type
prices        → vector name

description:
A vector must be declared before it can be used. A vector declaration specifies the data type of the elements the vector will store and the name of the vector.

Unlike a traditional array, a vector does not require a size when it is declared. An empty vector can be created and elements can be added later.

A vector may also be created with an initial number of elements. When only the size is provided, the elements are value-initialized. Numeric elements are initialized to 0.

A vector can also be initialized with values using an initializer list. The number of values in the initializer list determines the vector's initial size.

Another form allows a vector to be created with a specified number of elements that all begin with the same value.

Because vectors can grow and shrink while the program is running, the number of elements stored in a vector can change after it is declared.
examples:
Create five elements with the same starting value:

vector<int> scores(5, 100);

The vector contains:
100, 100, 100, 100, 100

Declare and initialize a vector of strings:

vector<string> names = {"Alex", "Jordan", "Taylor"};

description:
Individual elements of a vector can be accessed using an index. Like arrays, vectors use zero-based indexing, so the first element is at index 0, the second element is at index 1, and so on.

There are two common ways to access an individual vector element: the subscript operator ([ ]) and the at() member function.

The subscript operator places the index inside square brackets after the vector name. For example, scores[2] accesses the element at index 2, which is the thirdelement of the vector.

The at() function provides another way to access an element. The index is passed to the function as an argument. For example, scores.at(2) accesses the same element as scores[2].

An important difference is that at() performs bounds checking. If the specified index is outside the valid range of the vector, at() throws an exception. The subscript operator does not perform bounds checking.

Once an element has been accessed, it behaves much like a regular variable. Its value can be displayed, assigned a new value, used in an expression, or compared with another value.

The index may be a literal value, a variable, or an expression. This allows a loop control variable to be used as the index when traversing a vector.

For a vector containing n elements, the valid indexes are 0 through n - 1. The size() function can be used to determine the current number of elements in the vector.
syntax:
Using the subscript operator:

vectorName[index]

Using at():

vectorName.at(index)

Assign a value:

vectorName[index] = value;
vectorName.at(index) = value;
examples:
Modify an element using at():

scores.at(2) = 80;

description:
Vector traversal means accessing the elements of a vector one at a time, typically from the beginning of the vector to the end.

Traversing a vector is similar to traversing an array. A traditional for loop can use an index to access each element of the vector. A while loop or other loop can also be used when appropriate.

Vectors can also be traversed using a range-based for loop, which accesses each element without requiring an index. Iterators provide another way to move through the elements of a vector.

The choice of traversal method depends on what the program needs to do. An index-based loop is useful when the element's position is needed, while a range-based for loop is convenient when each element simply needs to be processed. Iterators are commonly used with Standard Library functions and algorithms.

Because basic traversal using loops is covered with arrays and looping structures, those topics can be used for additional information about the traversal process.

Bounds checking is the process of verifying that an index is within the valid range of a collection before accessing an element.

For arrays and vectors, valid indexes begin at 0 and end at one less than the number of elements. For example, a collection containing five elements has valid indexes from 0 through 4.

Accessing an element with an index outside the valid range is called an out-of-bounds access.

Traditional C++ arrays do not automatically perform bounds checking when the subscript operator ([ ]) is used. Accessing an array outside its valid range results in undefined behavior and may produce incorrect results, corrupt data, or cause the program to fail.

Vectors also allow elements to be accessed with the subscript operator ([ ]), which does not perform bounds checking.

The vector at() member function does perform bounds checking. If the requested index is outside the valid range, at() throws an exception rather than allowing the invalid access.

Loops that traverse arrays or vectors should use conditions that prevent the index from reaching the size of the collection. For a collection containing size elements, the normal condition is index < size, not index <= size.
syntax:
Valid index range:

0 through size - 1

Typical traversal condition:

index < size

Vector access with bounds checking:

vectorName.at(index)
examples:
Valid and invalid array indexes:

int scores[5];

scores[0] = 85;   // Valid
scores[4] = 92;   // Valid
scores[5] = 78;   // Out of bounds

description:
Dynamic resizing is the ability of a vector to change the number of elements it contains while a program is running.

Unlike a traditional array, whose size is fixed when it is created, a vector can grow or shrink as elements are added or removed.

A vector keeps track of both its size and its capacity. The size represents the number of elements currently stored in the vector. The capacity represents the number of elements the vector can currently store without allocating additional memory.

A vector may therefore have a capacity that is larger than its size. The unused capacity provides room for additional elements without requiring new memory to be allocated every time an element is added.

For example:

Size:      3
Capacity:  5

          +------+------+------+------+------+
Vector:   |  10  |  20  |  30  |      |      |
          +------+------+------+------+------+
             Elements        Available Space

If another element is added while unused capacity is available, the element can be placed in the existing storage and the vector's size increases.

When an element is added and the vector no longer has enough capacity, the vector must allocate a larger block of memory. The existing elements are moved or copied into the new storage, the old storage is released, and the new element is added.

This process is called reallocation. Reallocation requires additional work, so vectors typically allocate more space than is immediately required. This allows several elements to be added before another reallocation is necessary.

The amount by which capacity increases is determined by the C++ implementation. A program should not assume that the capacity will increase by a particular amount or that it will always double.

Removing elements decreases the vector's size, but it does not necessarily decrease its capacity. The vector may keep the allocated storage available for elements that are added later.

Functions such as push_back(), pop_back(), and resize() can change the number of elements in a vector. The size() and capacity() functions can be used to examine the vector's current size and storage capacity.

A vector's size and capacity describe two different properties of the vector.

The size is the number of elements that currently exist in the vector. The size() function returns this value.

The capacity is the number of elements the vector's currently allocated storage can hold before additional memory must be allocated. The capacity() function returns this value.

The capacity of a vector is always greater than or equal to its size, but the two values do not have to be equal.

For example:

Size:      3
Capacity:  5

          +------+------+------+------+------+
Vector:   |  10  |  20  |  30  |      |      |
          +------+------+------+------+------+
             Elements        Available Storage

The first three locations contain vector elements and are included in the size. The two remaining locations represent available storage and are included in the capacity, but they are not currently vector elements and cannot be accessed as if they were.

Adding an element increases the size. If sufficient capacity already exists, the capacity may remain unchanged. If the vector does not have enough capacity, additional storage is allocated and the capacity increases.

Removing elements decreases the size but does not normally decrease the capacity. The allocated storage may remain available for future elements.

A useful way to remember the difference is:
Size = how many elements exist.
Capacity = how many elements can fit in the currently allocated storage.

A vector's size is the number of elements that currently exist in the vector. The size() member function returns this value.

Because vectors can grow and shrink while a program is running, their size can change after they are created.

The resize() member function changes the number of elements in the vector.

If resize() increases the vector's size, new elements are added to the end of the vector. For numeric data types, the new elements are initialized to 0 unless another initial value is supplied.

If resize() decreases the vector's size, elements are removed from the end of the vector.

Changing the size may also cause the vector's capacity to increase if additional storage is required. Decreasing the size does not normally decrease the capacity.

The size of a vector represents actual elements that can be accessed using valid indexes from 0 through size() - 1.

The clear() member function removes all elements from a vector, reducing its size to 0. Unlike resize(), which can increase or decrease the number of elements to a specified size, clear() removes every element from the vector.

Calling clear() does not normally reduce the vector's capacity. The storage that was allocated for the vector may remain available so that new elements can be added later without immediately requiring additional memory allocation.

A vector's capacity is the number of elements that can fit in its currently allocated storage before additional memory must be allocated. The capacity() member function returns this value.

A vector's capacity may be greater than its size. The extra capacity represents storage that is available for future elements but does not currently contain vector elements.

The reserve() member function requests enough storage for at least a specified number of elements. Reserving capacity does not create new elements and does not change the vector's size.

For example, reserve(100) may increase the vector's capacity to at least 100, but the vector may still contain zero elements.

reserve() is useful when the programmer knows approximately how many elements will eventually be added. Reserving enough storage in advance can reduce the number of reallocations that occur as the vector grows.

If reserve() requests a capacity that is less than or equal to the vector's current capacity, the vector's storage does not need to change.

The exact capacity of a vector is controlled by the C++ implementation. A program should not assume that capacity will increase by a particular amount.

Removing elements or reducing the vector's size does not normally reduce its capacity. The allocated storage may remain available for future elements.

The shrink_to_fit() member function requests that the vector reduce its capacity to eliminate unused storage. It is commonly used when a vector's capacity is significantly larger than its size and the extra storage is no longer needed.

Unlike reserve(), which can be used to request additional storage, shrink_to_fit() requests that unnecessary storage be released.

Calling shrink_to_fit() does not change the number of elements in the vector. It affects capacity rather than size.

shrink_to_fit() is a request rather than a guarantee. The C++ implementation is not required to reduce the vector's capacity when the function is called.

Vectors can grow and shrink while a program is running by adding and removing elements.

The push_back() member function adds a new element to the end of a vector. The vector's size increases by one.

The pop_back() member function removes the last element from a vector. The vector's size decreases by one. pop_back() does not return the value that was removed.

The insert() member function adds an element at a specified position in the vector. Elements at and after that position are shifted toward the end of the vector to make room for the new element.

The erase() member function removes an element at a specified position. Elements after the removed element are shifted toward the beginning of the vector to fill the empty position.

A position for insert() or erase() can be specified using begin() and the + operator. For example, numbers.begin() + 2 identifies the element at index 2.

Adding or removing elements changes the size of the vector. Adding elements may also increase the vector's capacity if additional storage is required. Removing elements does not normally decrease the vector's capacity.

push_back() and pop_back() are useful when working with the end of a vector. insert() and erase() are useful when an element needs to be added or removed at another position.

Vectors can be passed to functions as arguments, used as function parameters, and returned from functions.

Unlike traditional arrays, vectors are passed by value by default. When a vector is passed by value, the function receives a copy of the vector. Changes made to the copy inside the function do not affect the original vector.

This is an important difference between vectors and traditional arrays. When a traditional array is passed to a function, changes made to its elements inside the function affect the original array. A vector does not behave this way unless it is explicitly passed by reference.

A vector can be passed by reference by placing an ampersand (&) with the parameter type. When a vector is passed by reference, the function works with the original vector rather than a copy. Changes made to the vector inside the function therefore affect the original vector.

If a function only needs to read a vector and should not modify it, the vector can be passed by constant reference using const and &. This avoids copying the vector while also preventing the function from changing it.

Because a vector may contain many elements, passing a large vector by value requires copying those elements. Passing the vector by constant reference is commonly used when the function only needs to examine the vector.

However, pass-by-reference should not be used automatically for every parameter. The method used should reflect what the function needs to do: use pass-by-value when a separate copy is appropriate, pass-by-reference when the function needs to modify the original vector, and pass-by-constant-reference when the function only needs to read the original vector without making a copy.

Unlike traditional arrays, a vector knows its own size. A separate size parameter is therefore normally unnecessary because the function can use the vector's size() member function.

Vectors can also be returned from value-returning functions. The function's return type specifies the vector type being returned.

Arrays and vectors both store collections of elements of the same data type and allow individual elements to be accessed using indexes beginning at 0. However, they differ in how their size, storage, functions, and parameter passing are handled.

The primary difference is that a traditional array has a fixed size, while a vector can dynamically change its number of elements while the program is running.

Arrays are useful when the number of elements is known and will remain fixed. Their simple structure also makes them useful for learning fundamental programming concepts such as indexing, traversal, searching, sorting, and how collections of data are stored.

Vectors are useful when the number of elements may change or is not known in advance. They provide member functions for adding and removing elements, changing the number of elements, checking the size, and managing storage.

Another important difference occurs when arrays and vectors are passed to functions. A traditional array parameter provides access to the original array elements, so changes made to those elements inside the function affect the original array. A vector follows normal C++ parameter passing rules and is passed by value by default, creating a copy unless it is explicitly passed by reference.

Traditional arrays also do not carry their size information when passed to a function, so the size is commonly passed as a separate parameter. A vector keeps track of its own size, which can be obtained using size().

Vectors also provide the at() member function, which performs bounds checking. Accessing either an array or vector with the subscript operator ([ ]) does not perform bounds checking.

Resource limitations may also affect the choice between an array and a vector. Vectors provide additional capabilities such as dynamic resizing and automatic storage management, but these capabilities can require additional memory and processing. In small embedded systems or other systems with very limited resources, the predictable size and lower overhead of a traditional array may make it a better choice when the number of elements is known in advance.

The choice between an array and a vector should be based on the needs of the program. If the number of elements is fixed and known, an array may be appropriate. If the collection needs to grow or shrink, or if the number of elements is not known in advance, a vector is generally the more appropriate choice.

Arrays vs Vectors

Arrays
├── Fixed number of elements
├── Cannot directly grow or shrink
├── Uses [ ] to access elements
├── Does not provide member functions such as size()
├── Size is commonly passed separately to functions
├── Function parameters provide access to original elements
├── Lower management overhead
└── Best when size is known and remains fixed

Vectors
├── Dynamic number of elements
├── Can grow and shrink while the program runs
├── Uses [ ] or at() to access elements
├── Keeps track of its own size and capacity
├── Provides functions for managing elements and storage
├── Does not normally need a separate size parameter
├── Passed by value by default
├── Additional overhead for dynamic storage management
└── Best when size may change or is not known in advance

Vectors can be searched using the same general techniques used with arrays, including linear search, binary search, std::find(), and std::binary_search().

The logic of the search does not change simply because the values are stored in a vector instead of an array. For example, a linear search still examines elements one at a time until the desired value is found, and a binary search still requires the data to be sorted before the search begins.

When using standard library search functions with a vector, the range is commonly specified using begin() and end().

Because the search algorithms themselves are covered in the array searching topics, refer to those topics for the full algorithms and examples.

Vectors can be sorted using the same general sorting techniques used with arrays, including bubble sort, selection sort, and the std::sort() function.

The logic of bubble sort and selection sort is the same when working with a vector because vector elements can be accessed by index in much the same way as array elements.

When using std::sort() with a vector, begin() and end() are commonly used to specify the range of elements to sort.

Because the sorting algorithms themselves are covered in the array sorting topics, refer to those topics for the full algorithms and examples.

A structure is a user-defined data type that groups related variables together into a single unit.

Unlike an array or vector, which stores multiple values of the same data type, a structure can contain related variables of different data types. The variables contained within a structure are called members.

For example, information about a student might include a name, student ID, and grade. These values have different data types, but they all describe the same student and can therefore be grouped together in a Student structure.

A structure can be visualized as a collection of related members:

Student
├── name       → string
├── studentID  → int
└── grade      → double

Defining a structure creates a new data type. After the structure has been defined, variables of that structure type can be declared. Each structure variable contains its own set of the members defined by the structure.

Structures can be used as an alternative to parallel arrays when several related pieces of data describe the same object. Instead of storing each attribute in a separate array, a structure groups the related values together into a single record. See Structures vs Parallel Arrays for a comparison of the two approaches.

keywords: Difference between structures and parallel arrays
description:
Parallel arrays and structures can both be used to organize related data, but they organize that data in different ways.

Parallel arrays store each attribute in a separate array. The relationship between the values is maintained by their indexes. Values at the same index represent information about the same object.

For example:

Parallel Arrays

Index       names        grades
  0         Alex           92
  1         Jordan         85
  2         Taylor         96

names[0] and grades[0] describe Alex, while names[1] and grades[1] describe Jordan. The programmer must make sure that the indexes of the parallel arrays remain synchronized.

Structures organize the data differently. Instead of grouping all names together and all grades together, a structure groups all of the information describing one object together.

Structures

students[0]
├── name  → Alex
└── grade → 92

students[1]
├── name  → Jordan
└── grade → 85

students[2]
├── name  → Taylor
└── grade → 96

With parallel arrays, the relationship between values is based on matching indexes. With structures, the related values are members of the same structure variable.

Structures often make programs easier to understand and maintain because the data describing an object is kept together. Adding another attribute, such as a student's major, requires adding another parallel array when using parallel arrays. With a structure, another member can be added to the structure definition.

Parallel arrays can still be appropriate for simple programs or situations where separate collections of individual values are useful. Structures are generally more appropriate when several related values together represent a single object or record.

Parallel Arrays vs Structures

Parallel Arrays
├── Each attribute is stored in a separate array
├── Related values are connected by matching indexes
├── Arrays must remain synchronized
├── Adding an attribute requires another array
└── Useful for simple collections of related data

Structures
├── Related attributes are grouped into one data type
├── Each object contains its own related values
├── Relationships do not depend on separate arrays staying synchronized
├── Adding an attribute means adding another structure member
└── Useful when multiple values describe one object or record

Defining a structure creates a new user-defined data type that groups related variables together. A structure is defined using the struct keyword, followed by the name of the structure and a set of braces containing its members.

Each member is declared with its own data type and name. The members of a structure can have different data types because they represent different attributes of the same type of object or record.

The structure definition ends with a semicolon after the closing brace. Forgetting this semicolon is a common syntax error.

Defining a structure does not create a variable or store data for an individual object. It defines the structure and members that variables of that type will contain.

For example, defining a Student structure creates a new Student data type. A separate declaration is then used to create a variable of the Student type.

The terms defining and declaring are sometimes confused. Defining a structure describes the new data type and its members. Declaring a structure variable creates a variable of that type.
examples:
The structure definition creates the Student data type:

Student
├── name       → string
├── studentID  → int
└── grade      → double

No Student variable has been created yet.

description:
After a structure has been defined, variables of the structure type can be declared. A structure variable contains its own set of the members specified by the structure definition.

A structure variable is declared by using the structure name as the data type, followed by the variable name. This is similar to declaring a variable using a built-in data type.

For example, if Student has already been defined as a structure, Student student1; declares a variable named student1 whose data type is Student.

A structure variable can also be initialized when it is declared by providing starting values for its members.

One method is aggregate initialization, where values are placed inside braces in the same order that the members are defined in the structure. Because aggregate initialization depends on member order, each value must correspond to the appropriate member in the structure definition.

C++20 also supports designated initializers, which identify each member by name using the member name preceded by a dot (.). This makes it clear which value initializes each member.

Designated initializers identify structure members by name. In standard C++20, the members that are initialized must appear in the same order that they are declared in the structure. However, depending on the C++ version, compiler, and compiler configuration being used, some compilers may allow designated initializers to appear in a different order. Because support and behavior can vary, maintaining the order in which the members are declared provides the greatest compatibility between C++ compilers.

Defining a structure and declaring a structure variable are different operations. Defining the structure creates the data type and specifies its members. Declaring a structure variable creates an individual variable of that type.
examples:
Declare and initialize a Student variable:

Student student1 = {"Alex", 12345, 92.5};

Declare and initialize using designated initializers:

Student student1 = {.name = "Alex", .studentID = 12345, .grade = 92.5};

description:
The members of a structure are accessed using the structure variable's name followed by the dot operator (.) and the name of the member.

Each member can be accessed individually and used much like a regular variable. A structure member can be assigned a value, displayed, used in an expression, or passed to a function.

If multiple variables are declared from the same structure, each structure variable has its own members. The structure variable name identifies which object's data is being accessed.
syntax: structureVariable.memberName

description:
The dot operator (.) is used to access a member of a structure or object.

The name of the structure variable or object is placed before the dot, and the name of the member being accessed is placed after the dot.

The dot operator can be used to access member variables and, with objects, call public member functions.

For more information about using the dot operator, see Accessing Structure Members and Member Functions.

Structures can be stored in arrays and vectors just like built-in data types. Instead of each element containing a single value such as an int or double, each element contains a complete structure variable with all of its members.

An array of structures stores a fixed number of structure variables. A vector of structures stores a collection of structure variables that can grow or shrink while the program is running.

For example, if Student is a structure containing name, studentID, and grade, an array or vector of Student objects can be used to store information about multiple students.

An array of structures can be visualized as:

students
├── [0]
│   ├── name      → Alex
│   ├── studentID → 1001
│   └── grade     → 92.5
├── [1]
│   ├── name      → Jordan
│   ├── studentID → 1002
│   └── grade     → 85.0
└── [2]
    ├── name      → Taylor
    ├── studentID → 1003
    └── grade     → 96.0

Accessing a member requires identifying both the element in the array or vector and the member within that structure. The subscript operator ([ ]) identifies the element, and the dot operator (.) identifies the member.

Arrays and vectors of structures are especially useful when a program needs to store multiple records containing the same types of related information. They provide a more organized alternative to maintaining several parallel arrays.

The choice between an array and a vector of structures follows the same general rules as other arrays and vectors. An array is appropriate when the number of records is known and fixed, while a vector is generally more appropriate when the number of records may change or is not known in advance.
examples:
Add another structure to a vector:

students.push_back({"Morgan", 1004, 88.5});

description:
Structures can be passed to functions as arguments, used as function parameters, and returned from functions.

Structures are passed by value by default. When a structure is passed by value, the function receives a copy of the structure variable and all of its members. Changes made to the copy inside the function do not affect the original structure variable.

A structure can be passed by reference by placing an ampersand (&) with the parameter type. When passed by reference, the function works with the original structure variable. Changes made to its members inside the function therefore affect the original variable.

If a function only needs to read the members of a structure and should not modify them, the structure can be passed by constant reference using const and &. This avoids making a copy while preventing the function from changing the original structure.

The method used to pass a structure should reflect what the function needs to do. Pass-by-value can be used when the function should work with a separate copy, pass-by-reference can be used when the function needs to modify the original structure, and pass-by-constant-reference can be used when the function only needs to read the original structure without making a copy.

Because defining a structure creates a user-defined data type, the structure name can also be used as a function's return type. This allows a function to create or obtain a complete structure variable and return it to the calling function.

Returning a structure can be especially useful when a function needs to produce several related values. Instead of returning the values separately, the values can be grouped into a structure and returned as a single value.

Structures therefore follow the same general function rules as other data types. They can be parameters, arguments, and return values.

A class is a user-defined data type that groups related data and the functions that operate on that data into a single unit. Classes are one of the fundamental concepts of object-oriented programming (OOP).

The data stored within a class describes the characteristics or state of an object. These variables are commonly called data members, member variables, or instance variables. The functions defined for a class describe the behaviors or operations that objects of the class can perform and are called member functions.

A class defines what data and behaviors objects of that type will have, but defining a class does not create an object. An object is an individual instance of a class.

For example, a Student class might describe students using a name, student ID, and grade, along with functions for displaying or modifying that information.

The relationship between a class and its objects can be visualized as:

Student Class
├── Data
│   ├── name
│   ├── studentID
│   └── grade
│
└── Behaviors
    ├── displayStudent()
    └── updateGrade()

                 ↓ creates objects of this type

student1
├── name      → Alex
├── studentID → 1001
└── grade     → 92.5

student2
├── name      → Jordan
├── studentID → 1002
└── grade     → 85.0

Both student1 and student2 are objects of the Student class. Each object has its own values for the instance variables, while both objects have the behaviors defined by the Student class.

A common way to think about the relationship is that a class acts as a blueprint or definition for a type of object, while an object is a specific instance created from that definition.

Classes are similar to structures because both can group related data into a user-defined data type. Classes extend this idea by commonly combining the data describing an object with the functions that operate on that data.

Classes also support concepts such as encapsulation and data hiding. The internal data of an object can be protected from direct access, while member functions provide controlled ways to interact with that data. This allows the class to separate how an object is used from the details of how it is implemented.

Classes allow programs to model related data and behavior as objects, helping organize larger programs into meaningful and reusable components.

Structures and classes are both used to group related data into organized, user-defined data types. Structures provide a major improvement over approaches such as parallel arrays because all of the information describing one object can be stored together.

For example, a Student structure might group a student's name, ID, GPA, and degree program into one organized unit rather than storing each piece of information in a separate parallel array.

Classes build on this same idea. A class can be thought of as an upgraded structure. Like a structure, a class groups related data together, but a class also groups the functions that operate on that data with the object itself.

For example, a Student structure could store a student's information, but functions used to calculate honors status, update a transcript, or display student information would normally be separate from the structure. With a class, those related functions can become part of the Student type itself.

Combining related data and behavior into the same type is one of the central ideas of object-oriented programming (OOP). It allows programs to model real-world objects more naturally and helps keep related code organized and easier to maintain.

When moving from structures to classes, many ideas remain familiar. Both structures and classes can contain fields, also called attributes or member variables, that describe the data associated with an object.

Classes also contain functions, commonly called methods or member functions, that describe what an object can do. These functions operate on the data that belongs to the object.

Classes also allow access to data and functions to be controlled using public and private sections. This allows the programmer to protect internal data and provide controlled ways for other parts of the program to interact with an object.

Classes can also provide more control over how objects are created, copied, and destroyed, making them well suited for larger and more complex software systems.

A class is a user-defined data type that describes the data and functions that objects of that type can have. An object is a variable, or instance, created from a class.

A class acts as the definition for a type, while an object is a specific instance of that type created in a program.

Multiple objects can be created from the same class. Each object has its own copy of the class's non-static member variables, so the objects can store different values while sharing the same class definition.

A simple way to remember the difference is: the class defines the type; an object is an instance of that type.
syntax: ClassName objectName;

description:
A class is made up of several components that define the data an object stores and the behaviors that objects of the class can perform.

In this course, a class is separated into a specification file and an implementation file. The specification file (.hpp or .h) describes what the class contains and what it can do, while the implementation file (.cpp) contains the definitions that describe how its member functions perform their operations.

The major components of a class include the class name, access specifiers, instance variables, constructors, and member functions. These components are organized between the specification and implementation files.

Class
|
|-- Specification File (.hpp / .h)
|   |
|   |-- Class Name
|   |      Identifies the user-defined data type.
|   |
|   |-- Access Specifiers
|   |      Control access to members of the class.
|   |
|   |-- Instance Variables
|   |      Store the data that describes each object.
|   |
|   |-- Constructor Prototypes
|   |      Declare how objects can be initialized.
|   |
|   \-- Member Function Prototypes
|          Declare the behaviors available to objects.
|
\-- Implementation File (.cpp)
    |
    |-- Constructor Definitions
    |      Define how objects are initialized.
    |
    \-- Member Function Definitions
           Define how the class behaviors are performed.

The class name defines the new data type. Objects created from the class are individual instances of that type.

Instance variables hold the data that belongs to each object. Each object has its own values for these variables.

Member functions operate on the object's data and describe what the object can do. Constructors are special member functions that help establish the object's initial state.

Access specifiers such as public and private control how the members of the class can be accessed. Instance variables are commonly placed in the private section, while constructors and other member functions that need to be used outside the class are commonly placed in the public section.

Together, these components allow a class to combine data, behavior, and access control into a single user-defined type.

Separating the specification from the implementation supports abstraction. The specification file describes what the class contains and what operations are available, while the implementation file contains the details of how those operations are performed. A programmer using the class does not need to know the implementation details in order to use it.

Defining a class creates a new user-defined data type that describes the data and behaviors that objects of the class will have.

A class is defined using the class keyword followed by the class name. The members of the class are placed inside braces, and the class definition ends with a semicolon.

The members of a class can include instance variables, constructors, and member functions. Access specifiers such as public and private control how these members can be accessed.

In this course, classes are separated into a specification file (.hpp or .h) and an implementation file (.cpp). The specification file contains the class definition, including the instance variables and the prototypes for constructors and member functions. The implementation file contains the definitions of the constructors and member functions.

The specification file describes what the class contains and what the class can do. The implementation file describes how those operations are performed. Keeping the specification and implementation separate supports abstraction by separating what is available from the details of how it is implemented.

Defining a class does not create an object. It creates the data type that will be used later to declare objects of that class.

After a class has been defined, variables of the class type can be declared. A variable created from a class is called an object or an instance of the class.

A class variable is declared by using the class name as the data type followed by the variable name. This follows the same general pattern used to declare variables of built-in and other user-defined data types.

When an object is created, a constructor for the class is automatically called. The constructor is responsible for establishing the initial state of the object.

If the class provides a default constructor, an object can be declared without providing arguments. If the class provides a constructor with parameters, values can be supplied when the object is created to initialize its instance variables.

Each object is a separate instance of the class and contains its own values for the instance variables. Creating multiple objects from the same class does not cause them to share the same instance variable values.

The class definition describes the type of object that can be created. Declaring a class variable creates an individual object of that type.

A constructor is a special member function that is automatically called when an object of a class is created. Its primary purpose is to initialize the object and establish its initial state.

A constructor has the same name as the class and does not have a return type, not even void. Because constructors are member functions, their prototypes are placed in the class definition in the specification file (.hpp or .h), while their definitions are placed in the implementation file (.cpp).

When an object is declared, the appropriate constructor is automatically called. The programmer does not call the constructor like a normal member function after creating the object. Object creation and constructor execution are part of the same process.

A class can have more than one constructor. Constructors can be overloaded by providing different parameter lists, allowing objects of the same class to be initialized in different ways.

A constructor that can be called without arguments is called a default constructor. A constructor that accepts values through parameters can be used to initialize an object's instance variables with values supplied when the object is created.

For example, a Student class might provide a default constructor that initializes a student with default values and another constructor that accepts a name, student ID, and grade. See Default Constructors and Parameterized Constructors.

Constructors help ensure that an object begins in a known and valid state instead of leaving its instance variables without appropriate initial values.

A default constructor is a constructor that can be called without passing any arguments. It is automatically called when an object is created without providing initialization values.

A default constructor is commonly used to place an object into a known initial state by assigning appropriate default values to its instance variables.

Like all constructors, a default constructor has the same name as the class and does not have a return type, not even void.

In this course, the prototype for the default constructor is placed in the public section of the class definition in the specification file (.hpp or .h). The constructor definition is placed in the implementation file (.cpp).

The constructor prototype does not contain parameters because no arguments are required. When an object is declared without arguments, the default constructor is automatically called.

If no constructors are declared for a class, C++ can provide an implicit default constructor. However, once a programmer declares another constructor, such as a parameterized constructor, C++ does not automatically provide the implicit default constructor. If objects should still be creatable without arguments, a default constructor must also be provided.

A parameterized constructor is a constructor that accepts one or more values through parameters. These values can be used to establish the initial state of an object when the object is created.

A parameterized constructor allows different objects of the same class to begin with different values. For example, different Student objects can be created with different names, student IDs, and grades.

The values supplied when the object is created are arguments. These arguments are passed to the constructor's parameters, which can then be used to initialize the object's instance variables.

Like all constructors, a parameterized constructor has the same name as the class and does not have a return type, not even void.

In this course, the constructor prototype is placed in the public section of the class definition in the specification file (.hpp or .h), while the constructor definition is placed in the implementation file (.cpp).

A class can contain multiple constructors with different parameter lists. This is constructor overloading and allows objects of the class to be initialized in different ways.

For Professor Raymond's class do not put parameter (variable) names in the constructor prototypes.

Constructor overloading occurs when a class has more than one constructor with different parameter lists. This allows objects of the same class to be initialized in different ways.

Constructor overloading follows the same rules as function overloading. The constructors have the same name because every constructor has the name of the class, but they must have different parameter lists. See Function Overloading for more information about how overloading works.

A common example is providing both a default constructor and a parameterized constructor. The constructor that is called is determined by the arguments provided when the object is created.

A member function is a function that belongs to a class and defines a behavior or operation that objects of the class can perform. Member functions are also commonly called methods.

Member functions can directly access the instance variables and other member functions of the class. This allows the behaviors of an object to work with the data that belongs to that object.

In this course, the prototype for a member function is placed in the class definition in the specification file (.hpp or .h), while the member function definition is placed in the implementation file (.cpp).

When a member function is defined outside of the class definition, the scope resolution operator (::) is used with the class name to identify the class to which the function belongs.

A public member function can be called from outside the class by using an object name, the dot operator (.), and the member function name. When the function is called through an object, it operates on the instance variables belonging to that object.

For example, if student1 and student2 are objects of the Student class, calling student1.displayStudent() displays the information belonging to student1, while calling student2.displayStudent() displays the information belonging to student2.

Member functions help keep the operations that work with an object's data together with the class that defines that data. This is an important part of organizing data and behavior using object-oriented programming.

Getters and setters are public member functions that provide controlled access to private instance variables. A getter retrieves the value of an instance variable, while a setter changes the value of an instance variable.

A getter, also called an accessor, usually returns the value of a private instance variable. It allows code outside the class to retrieve the value without providing direct access to the variable itself.

A setter, also called a mutator, usually receives a new value through a parameter and assigns that value to a private instance variable. Because the change occurs through a member function, the setter can validate the value before modifying the object's data.

For example, a Student class might have a private grade instance variable. A getGrade() function can return the current grade, while a setGrade() function can change the grade. The setter can also verify that the new grade is within an acceptable range before storing it.

Getters and setters support encapsulation and data hiding. The instance variables remain private, while the class provides a public interface for retrieving or modifying the data.

Not every instance variable must have both a getter and a setter. A class should provide only the operations that other parts of the program need. For example, an instance variable that should be readable but should not be changed from outside the class might have a getter but no setter.

Getters and Setters
|
|-- Getter (Accessor)
|   |-- Retrieves a value
|   |-- Usually returns the value
|   \-- Does not normally modify the instance variable
|
\-- Setter (Mutator)
    |-- Changes a value
    |-- Usually receives the new value as a parameter
    \-- Can validate the value before storing it

Access modifiers control where the members of a class can be accessed. They are used to control access to instance variables, constructors, and member functions.

The three access modifiers in C++ are public, private, and protected. In this class we will only discuss public and private.

Public members can be accessed from outside the class through an object. Constructors and member functions that form the public interface of a class are commonly placed in the public section.

Private members can only be accessed directly by member functions of the class and other specially permitted functions or classes. Instance variables are commonly placed in the private section so that outside code cannot directly modify the object's internal data.

Access modifiers are an important part of encapsulation and data hiding. By keeping instance variables private and providing public member functions to interact with them, a class can control how its data is accessed and modified.

For example, rather than making a grade instance variable public, the class can keep it private and provide public getGrade() and setGrade() member functions. The setter can then validate a new grade before changing the private instance variable.

In a C++ class, members are private by default if no access modifier is specified. However, explicitly writing public and private makes the organization and intended access of the class clearer.

Encapsulation and abstraction are two important concepts used when designing classes. They help organize a class and control how other parts of a program interact with it.

Encapsulation is the idea of grouping related data and the functions that operate on that data together within a class. The class becomes a single unit that represents both the data associated with an object and the behaviors that operate on that data.

Encapsulation also allows access to the internal data of an object to be controlled. Instance variables are commonly kept private, while public member functions provide the operations that other parts of the program are allowed to perform.

Abstraction is the idea of separating what something does from the details of how it does it. A programmer using an object only needs to know what public operations the class provides. The programmer does not need to know all of the details of how those operations are implemented.

The separation of a class into specification and implementation files helps demonstrate abstraction. The specification file (.hpp or .h) describes the class and the operations that are available, while the implementation file (.cpp) contains the details of how those operations are performed.

For example, a Student class might provide a public setGrade() member function. Code using a Student object only needs to know that setGrade() can be used to change the grade. The details of validating and storing the grade are handled by the class.

The concepts can be summarized as:

Encapsulation
├── Groups related data and functions together
├── Keeps the parts of an object organized
├── Commonly keeps instance variables private
└── Provides public functions for interacting with the object

Abstraction
├── Focuses on what an object can do
├── Hides unnecessary implementation details
├── Specification file describes what is available
└── Implementation file describes how it works

Objects can be stored in arrays and vectors just like values of other data types. Instead of each element containing a single value, each element contains a complete object of the specified class.

An array of objects stores a fixed number of objects, while a vector of objects stores a collection of objects that can grow or shrink while the program is running.

Each element in the array or vector is a separate object. Each object has its own values for the instance variables defined by the class, while all of the objects have the behaviors provided by the member functions of the class.

For example, if Student is a class, an array or vector of Student objects can be used to store and work with multiple students.

The subscript operator ([ ]) is used to identify an object in the array or vector. The dot operator (.) can then be used to call one of that object's public member functions.

Because instance variables are commonly private, code outside the class should normally interact with each object through its public member functions rather than directly accessing its instance variables.

The choice between an array and a vector of objects follows the same general rules as other arrays and vectors. An array is appropriate when the number of objects is known and fixed, while a vector is generally more appropriate when the number of objects may change or is not known in advance.

When an array of objects is declared with a size, a constructor that can be called without arguments is needed so that each object in the array can be initialized. For example, declaring Student students[10]; causes a constructor to be called for each of the ten Student objects.

The same requirement applies when a vector is created with an initial size or when resize() increases the size of a vector. The new elements must be created and initialized, so the class must provide a constructor that can be called without arguments.

A default constructor is not required simply because objects are stored in an array or vector. If the objects are created using constructors with arguments and then added to a vector, for example, a default constructor may not be needed.
examples:
Create a vector of Student objects:

vector<Student> students;

description:
Once a class has been defined, variables of that class type can be declared. A variable created from a class is called an object, or an instance of the class.

An object is declared by specifying the class name followed by the object name, similar to declaring a variable using a built-in data type.

When an object is created, a constructor is automatically called to initialize the object. If the object is declared without arguments, a default constructor is used. If values are provided when the object is declared, a matching parameterized constructor can be used to initialize the object.

Multiple objects can be created from the same class. Each object has its own copy of the class's non-static member variables.
syntax:
ClassName objectName;

ClassName objectName(arguments);
examples:
Declare a Student object using the default constructor:
Student student1;

Declare and initialize a Student object using a parameterized constructor:
Student student2("Alex", 12345, 3.75);

description:
A namespace is a named scope used to organize related identifiers and help prevent naming conflicts in a program. Variables, functions, classes, and other identifiers can be placed inside a namespace.

As programs become larger or use multiple libraries, it is possible for different parts of a program to use the same identifier. Without namespaces, these duplicate names could cause conflicts because the compiler would not know which identifier is intended.

Namespaces solve this problem by placing identifiers into separate named scopes. Two namespaces can therefore contain identifiers with the same name because each identifier belongs to a different namespace.

For example, a Geometry namespace and a Statistics namespace could both contain a function named calculate(). The namespace identifies which calculate() function should be used, allowing both functions to exist in the same program without a naming conflict.

Namespaces also help organize related parts of a program. A Geometry namespace might contain functions and constants related to geometric calculations, while a Statistics namespace might contain functions related to statistical calculations.

The C++ Standard Library uses a namespace named std. Many identifiers that have been used throughout this course, including cout, cin, string, and vector, belong to the std namespace.

Namespaces can be visualized as:

Program
|
|-- Geometry Namespace
|   |-- area()
|   |-- perimeter()
|   \-- PI
|
\-- Statistics Namespace
    |-- mean()
    |-- median()
    \-- mode()

A namespace does not create an object or a new data type. Instead, it creates a named scope that groups identifiers and distinguishes them from identifiers with the same name in other scopes.

A namespace is defined using the namespace keyword followed by the name of the namespace. The identifiers that belong to the namespace are placed inside braces.

Variables, constants, functions, classes, and other identifiers can be defined or declared inside a namespace. These identifiers become members of the namespace.

Unlike a class or structure definition, a namespace definition does not end with a semicolon after the closing brace.

A namespace can be defined in more than one location. Additional definitions using the same namespace name add members to the existing namespace rather than creating a different namespace.

Namespaces are commonly used with user-defined header files to organize related functions, constants, and other identifiers while reducing the possibility of naming conflicts with other parts of a program or other libraries.

When function prototypes are declared inside a namespace, the function definitions can also be placed inside the namespace. Alternatively, the definitions can be placed outside the namespace by using the namespace name and scope resolution operator (::) with each function name. In either case, the functions remain members of the namespace.

For Professor Raymond's class you must use function prototypes in the namespace definition, and put the function definitions outside the namespace (the second syntax example).

Members of a namespace can be accessed by using the namespace name followed by the scope resolution operator (::) and the name of the member.

Using the namespace name with the scope resolution operator creates a qualified name. The qualified name identifies both the member being used and the namespace to which that member belongs.

For example, Geometry::circleArea identifies the circleArea() function that belongs to the Geometry namespace. Geometry::PI identifies the PI constant that belongs to the Geometry namespace.

Qualifying a member with its namespace is especially important when different namespaces contain members with the same name. The namespace name tells the compiler which member should be used.

The same syntax is used with members of the C++ Standard Library. For example, std::cout, std::string, and std::vector identify cout, string, and vector as members of the std namespace.

Using the namespace name and scope resolution operator makes it clear where an identifier comes from and helps prevent ambiguity when multiple namespaces contain the same identifier.
examples:
Access a constant from a namespace:

cout << Geometry::PI << endl;

description:
The standard namespace, named std, is the namespace used by the C++ Standard Library. Many of the identifiers used throughout C++ programs belong to the std namespace.

For example, cout, cin, endl, string, vector, and many other standard library identifiers are members of the std namespace. Their fully qualified names include std and the scope resolution operator (::), such as std::cout, std::cin, std::string, and std::vector.

The std namespace helps prevent naming conflicts between identifiers provided by the C++ Standard Library and identifiers created by programmers or other libraries.

Including a standard library header file and accessing the std namespace are two different operations. An #include directive makes the declarations from a header available to the program, while std:: identifies an item as a member of the standard namespace.

For example, #include <iostream> makes the declarations for input and output available to the program. The names cout and cin provided by that library belong to the std namespace and can be accessed as std::cout and std::cin.

Members of the std namespace can be accessed individually with the scope resolution operator, or a using declaration or using directive can be used to allow selected names or all names from the namespace to be used without the std:: qualification.
syntax:
Access a member of the standard namespace:

std::memberName

Examples:

std::cout
std::cin
std::string
std::vector

topic: Namespaces with Header and Implementation Files
description:
Namespaces can be used with header and implementation files to organize related functions, constants, and other identifiers while helping prevent naming conflicts.

When functions belong to a namespace, their prototypes can be placed inside the namespace in the header file. The function definitions are then placed in the implementation file.

The function definitions can be placed inside a namespace block in the implementation file. Alternatively, the definitions can be placed outside a namespace block by qualifying each function name with the namespace name and scope resolution operator (::).

When the NamespaceName::functionName() form is used, the function prototype must have already declared the function as a member of that namespace. Including the header file in the implementation file provides that declaration.

A program that uses the namespace includes the header file and accesses the namespace members using the namespace name and scope resolution operator.

This organization can be visualized as:

Geometry.hpp
└── namespace Geometry
    └── Function prototypes

Geometry.cpp
├── #include "Geometry.hpp"
└── Function definitions
    └── Geometry::functionName()

main.cpp
├── #include "Geometry.hpp"
└── Geometry::functionName()

A nested namespace is a namespace defined inside another namespace. Nested namespaces provide additional levels of organization when a namespace contains several related groups of identifiers.

For example, a Geometry namespace could contain an Area namespace and a Perimeter namespace. Functions that calculate area can be grouped inside Geometry::Area, while functions that calculate perimeter can be grouped inside Geometry::Perimeter.

Members of a nested namespace are accessed by specifying each namespace followed by the scope resolution operator (::).

Nested namespaces also allow different groups within the same namespace to contain members with the same name. For example, both Geometry::Area and Geometry::Perimeter could contain a circle() function because the functions belong to different scopes.

You have already encountered similar nested scope notation when working with file output. The append file mode can be written as std::ios::app. The scope resolution operators show that app is found within the ios scope, which is itself found within the std namespace. When using namespace std; is included in the program, the std portion does not need to be specified, so it can be written as ios::app.

Nested namespaces can be visualized as:

Geometry
|
|-- Area
|   |-- circle()
|   \-- rectangle()
|
\-- Perimeter
    |-- circle()
    \-- rectangle()

The fully qualified names identify the complete path to each member:

Geometry::Area::circle()
Geometry::Perimeter::circle()
relatedTopics: Namespaces with Header and Implementation Files

description:
Recursion is a problem-solving technique in which a problem is solved by repeatedly reducing it to smaller versions of the same problem.

In programming, recursion is commonly implemented using a function that calls itself. Each call works on a smaller or simpler version of the original problem until a condition is reached that can be solved without making another recursive call.

A recursive solution must eventually reach a stopping condition. Without a stopping condition, the recursive process would continue making additional function calls.

Recursion can be visualized as:

Original Problem
       ↓
Smaller Problem
       ↓
Smaller Problem
       ↓
Stopping Condition
       ↓
Results Return

Recursion is another way of performing repetition. Loops repeat statements within the same function, while recursion performs repetition through repeated function calls.

Some problems can be solved using either iteration or recursion. Recursion is especially useful when a problem can naturally be described in terms of smaller versions of itself.

A recursive function is a function that calls itself, either directly or through another function, as part of solving a problem.

Each time the function calls itself, a new function call begins with its own parameter values and local variables. The recursive call should work with a smaller or simpler version of the original problem.

A recursive function requires a condition that stops the recursive calls. This stopping condition is called the base case. The portion of the function that makes another recursive call is called the recursive case.

Each recursive call must make progress toward the base case. If the base case is never reached, the function will continue making recursive calls and can eventually cause a stack overflow.

Recursive functions follow the same general rules as other functions. They can receive values through parameters, use local variables, and return values. The important difference is that the function can call itself.
examples:
Call the recursive function:

countDown(3);

The recursive calls are:

countDown(3)
    ↓
countDown(2)
    ↓
countDown(1)
    ↓
countDown(0)
    ↓
Blastoff!

description:
A recursive function is generally made up of two important parts: a base case and a recursive case.

The base case is the condition that stops the recursion. When the base case is reached, the function completes without making another recursive call.

The recursive case is the portion of the function that calls the function again. The recursive call should use a modified argument that represents a smaller or simpler version of the problem.

It is important that each recursive call makes progress toward the base case. Simply having a base case is not enough if the recursive calls never reach it.

If a recursive function does not have a reachable base case, it can continue creating additional function calls until the program runs out of available stack space. This is called a stack overflow.

The relationship between the two cases can be summarized as:

Recursive Function
|
|-- Base Case
|   |-- Stops the recursion
|   \-- Does not make another recursive call
|
\-- Recursive Case
    |-- Makes another recursive call
    \-- Moves the problem toward the base case
examples:
The recursive calls move toward the base case:

countDown(3)
    ↓
countDown(2)
    ↓
countDown(1)
    ↓
countDown(0)  ← Base case
